rows.title: Environment - components; ecology, ecosystem, food chain and food web, energy flow, ecological pyramids
sub: Group-II M2-B-47: Basic concepts of ecology - habitat, niche, population, community and biome
Group-II M2-B-48: Ecosystem - components (biotic and abiotic), structure and function
Group-II M2-B-49: Types of ecosystems - forest, grassland, desert, aquatic (freshwater, marine, estuarine, wetland)
Group-II M2-B-50: Energy flow, food chains, food webs and ecological pyramids

secs.t: Energy flow - solar source, share captured, GPP vs NPP, ten percent law, productivity ranking

x: Exam angle: "most productive ecosystem" = tropical rainforest in APPSC keys.
Less than 50% of incident sunlight is photosynthetically active radiation, and plants fix only about 2–10% of that PAR.
On average, only about
of incoming solar energy is captured and used in photosynthesis as primary production efficiency.
GPP is the total organic matter produced through photosynthesis; NPP is GPP minus producer respiration; secondary productivity is new organic matter formed by consumers.
Raymond Lindeman formulated the ten per cent law in 1942.
Both statements are true, and the large energy loss at each transfer leaves insufficient energy to support many successive trophic levels.
Tropical rainforest
s are the standard highest-productivity ecosystem among the alternatives.
Open oceans have low productivity per unit area, but their enormous area gives them a large total output.

secs.t: Food chain types - grazing vs detritus, trophic levels, missing-level questions, food web

x: Exam angle: a "missing second trophic level" means no herbivore in the chain (e.g. tiger, grass, snake, frog); "correct grazing chain" means it starts with a producer and moves up in order.
A
detritus food chain
starts with dead organic matter such as leaf litter and proceeds through detritivores such as earthworms to higher consumers.
Phytoplankton are producers, zooplankton are primary consumers, and small and large fish occupy progressively higher trophic positions.
A trophic level is the functional position occupied by an organism in a food chain.
Both statements are true, and the interconnected nature of food chains explains why removal of one link can affect subsequent branches.
A food web is made up of interlinked food chains and therefore contains multiple connected feeding pathways, not a single unconnected pathway.

secs.t: Ecosystem components - biotic vs abiotic, decomposers, natural vs artificial

x: Bacteria and fungi
act as decomposers and convert dead organic matter into inorganic nutrients that can be reused by producers.
Decomposers release inorganic nutrients from dead organic matter, making them available again to producers and linking living and non-living components.
Humans are omnivores, saprotrophs feed on dead matter, reptiles are cold-blooded, and camels are adapted to desert conditions.
Phytoplankton are producers, zooplankton are consumers, and bacteria and fungi act as decomposers in a pond ecosystem.

secs.t: Ecology terms - habitat, niche, population attributes, community, biome, ecotone, resistance, resilience

x: A biome is a large region defined by
climate and dominant vegetation
, such as rainforest, tundra or desert.
An ecotone is a transition zone, and its boundary conditions may produce an edge effect and increased species richness.
Resilience
refers to the ability to recover after a disturbance, whereas resistance refers to withstanding it.

secs.t: Ecological pyramids - number, biomass, energy; upright and inverted cases

x: Exam angle: "which pyramid is inverted": pyramid of numbers in a parasitic chain; "which can never be inverted": the energy pyramid.
A tree ecosystem may have one producer tree supporting numerous herbivorous insects, producing an inverted pyramid of numbers.
Parasitic food chains can have fewer hosts supporting numerous parasites, resulting in an inverted pyramid of numbers.

secs.t: Producers in different ecosystems - terrestrial, aquatic, chemosynthetic

x: Herbs, shrubs and trees
are the principal producers in terrestrial ecosystems.
Aquatic producers include
phytoplankton, algae, and submerged and floating plants
Chemosynthetic bacteria, including sulphur bacteria, use chemical energy rather than light at deep-sea vents.

secs.t: Species roles - keystone, foundation, flagship, indicator, umbrella

x: A
keystone species
has an ecological effect far larger than its abundance; its removal may cause the community to collapse.
Pisaster ochraceus is a keystone sea star that
controls mussels in intertidal zones
A
flagship species
is a charismatic species used to draw public support for conservation; the tiger and giant panda are examples.

secs.t: Habitat adaptations - halophytes, xerophytes, hydrophytes

x: Halophytes may possess pneumatophores for breathing, salt glands and vivipary; mangrove plants such as Rhizophora are examples.
Xerophytes are adapted to deserts through features such as thick cuticles, sunken stomata, spines, succulence and CAM; Opuntia is an example.
Hydrophytes
are water plants and commonly possess aerenchyma, reduced roots, thin cuticles and floating leaves.

secs.t: Biotic interactions - mutualism to competition, coevolved pairs

x: Orchid on mango is commensalism, Cuscuta is parasitism and Penicillium inhibiting bacteria is amensalism.
Competition
has a -/- effect because both species are adversely affected while using the same limited resource.
The fig wasp pollinates the fig and obtains a breeding site, making the association a coevolved mutualistic relationship.
The Ophrys orchid attracts bees through sexual deceit, thereby facilitating pollination.
Resource partitioning permits competing species to coexist by using different portions of a resource, such as different parts of the same plant.

secs.t: Habitat vs niche - fundamental, realised, niche breadth, proponents

x: Fundamental niche is the potential range of conditions and resources available to a species when competition and other biological limitations are absent.
A realised niche is the portion of the fundamental niche actually used under competition and other ecological constraints.
G. E. Hutchinson
proposed the n-dimensional niche concept in 1957.

secs.t: Ecotone and edge effect - meaning, which habitats are ecotones

x: An ecotone is a transition zone between two biological communities or biomes, generally having intermediate conditions.
A uniform stand of one forest type is a single community, not an ecotone.
Grassland is identified as an ecotonal region between
forest and desert
conditions.
The increased bird density at a forest-desert boundary illustrates the
edge effect
and the occurrence of edge species.

secs.t: Population attributes - natality, mortality, density, age pyramids, growth curves, K, r/K

x: The S-curve represents logistic growth, in which population growth slows as it approaches carrying capacity K; it is expressed as dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K.
r-selected species generally produce many small offspring, provide little parental care and often inhabit unstable environments.
All three statements are correct. r-selected species include many insects and weeds, whereas elephants and humans illustrate the K-selected strategy of fewer offspring and greater care.

secs.t: Ecologists → contribution

x: Charles Elton
contributed to the understanding of food chains, ecological pyramids and ecological niches; the Eltonian pyramid is named after him.

Cowles studied succession on Lake Michigan sand dunes; Clements developed phases of succession and monoclimax theory; Tansley coined ecosystem; Odum contributed to ecosystem ecology and authored Fundamentals of Ecology.

secs.t: Ecogeographic rules → trait

x: Jordan's rule relates temperature to the number of vertebrae in fish; colder conditions are associated with a greater number of vertebrae.
Bergmann, Allen and Rensch respectively describe body size, appendage length and sexual size dimorphism.
Gloger’s rule relates climate to
colouration
; warm and humid environments are generally associated with darker colouration.

secs.t: Levels of ecological organisation - organism to biosphere

x: The ecological order is organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere.
The complete sequence proceeds from atoms to molecules, protoplasm, cells, tissues, organs, organisms, populations, communities, ecosystems, biomes and biosphere.
All three statements correctly describe the limits and functioning of the biosphere.

secs.t: Ecosystem as functional unit - term, definition, open vs closed, structure vs function

x: In 1935, Arthur Tansley described an ecosystem as a system resulting from the integration of all living and non-living factors of the environment.
Ecosystem structure includes the biotic community, abiotic materials, species composition and trophic levels.
Energy flow, nutrient cycling and self-regulation are all functional characteristics of ecosystems.
Energy flow in ecosystems obeys
the laws of thermodynamics

secs.t: Abiotic factors - climatic, edaphic, topographic; limiting-factor laws

x: An abiotic factor is
any non-living component that affects organisms or their environment
, such as light, temperature, water or soil.
Climatic factors include light, temperature and rainfall; edaphic factors relate to soil; topographic factors include altitude, slope and aspect.
Abiotic factors can either enable the distribution of organisms or limit it when conditions fall outside suitable ranges.

secs.t: Ecosystem stability - resistance, resilience, homeostasis

x: Homeostasis is the self-regulatory capacity by which an ecosystem resists stress through feedback up to a limit.
Resilience
is the ability of an ecosystem to recover after a disturbance.

secs.t: Decomposition - steps, organisms, factors

x: Decomposition proceeds through fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation.
Detritivores such as
earthworm
s fragment detritus into smaller particles, facilitating subsequent decomposition processes.
Bacteria and fungi are the principal decomposers, while earthworms, nematodes and arthropods act as helpers.
Decomposition is rapid when detritus contains nitrogen and sugars and the climate is warm and moist.

secs.t: Autotroph types - photoautotrophs, chemoautotrophs, archaea

x: Photoautotrophs use sunlight and include green plants, algae and cyanobacteria.
Chemoautotrophic bacteria in deep ocean trenches can use
hydrogen sulphide
released from cracks on the sea floor as an energy source.
Nitrifying bacteria are chemoautotrophs, and many chemoautotrophic archaea such as methanogens inhabit extreme environments.

secs.t: Environment - meaning, composite nature, categories

x: Environment comprises
the surroundings and conditions in which organisms live
Lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere constitute the physical category.
The cultural environment is man-made and includes social, economic and political aspects.
A habitat is a living place suited to a species, whereas environment is broader and may include conditions without life.

secs.t: Ecosystem classification - natural vs artificial, terrestrial vs aquatic, stability

x: Tundra, forest, grassland, desert and mountain are all terrestrial ecosystem types.
Mangroves form an ecotone joining marine and terrestrial ecosystems.
The edge effect
refers to the richer species density commonly found in an ecotone or boundary zone.
Diverse and complex systems such as
rainforest
s are generally more stable than simple systems such as tundra, deserts and monoculture croplands.

secs.t: Marine ecosystem - zones, coral reefs, plankton, hydrothermal vents

x: Exam angle: "which does NOT belong to marine ecosystems": rivers and freshwater lakes do not; coral reefs, hydrothermal vents and tidal zones do.
The name chiefly refers to their exceptionally high species richness; wave breaking and erosion control are additional functions and do not explain the entire comparison.
Hydrothermal vents are deep-sea habitats where chemosynthetic bacteria form the base of food chains in the absence of sunlight.

secs.t: Wetlands - types, functions, hydrophyte adaptations, Ramsar, World Wetlands Day

x: Flood moderation, water purification, biodiversity conservation and carbon storage are all important wetland functions.
Aerenchyma
is air-filled tissue that helps aquatic plants transport gases within submerged or waterlogged parts.
Reduced roots, a thin cuticle and upper-surface stomata on floating leaves are hydrophyte adaptations.
The Ramsar framework promotes site designation and wise use; threatened sites may be placed on the Montreux Record.

secs.t: Freshwater - lentic vs lotic, lake zonation, trophic status

x: Lentic ecosystems contain still water, including
pond
s, lakes, pools, ditches and marshes.
The
littoral zone
is the shallow edge of a lake where light reaches the bottom and rooted plants commonly grow.
The profundal zone lies below the limnetic zone, is deep and dark, does not support photosynthesis, and is associated with decomposers.

secs.t: Estuaries and mangroves - salinity gradient, halophytes, climate role, Indian estuaries

x: Salinity generally increases from near-freshwater conditions upstream to approximately 35 ppt near the sea-facing mouth.
An estuary is an ecotone because it forms a transition zone between freshwater and saltwater environments.
Halophytes tolerate saline conditions, and salt-excreting glands, succulent leaves, pneumatophores and vivipary are important adaptations found among estuarine and mangrove plants.
Mangroves buffer cyclones and storm surges, reduce coastal erosion and store carbon.

secs.t: Grassland ecosystems - regional names; Indian grasslands and states

x: Shola consists of high-altitude grasslands and stunted forests in
the Western Ghats of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu
Terai refers to tall wet grasslands along the Himalayan foothills, including areas of Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Assam.
Banni is about 2,600 sq km, has been a Reserve Forest since 1955, supports Maldhari pastoralists and Banni buffalo, and is threatened by invasive Prosopis juliflora.

secs.t: Forest ecosystems - types and features

x: Tropical rainforest
s have the highest species richness among terrestrial ecosystems.
Rapid litter decay in tropical rainforests leaves the soil relatively thin and nutrient-poor.
Taiga forests have slow decomposition, which produces thick litter and acidic soil.
In mature forests, photosynthesis and respiration approximately balance with respect to net oxygen production, but the forests continue to function as important carbon sinks.

secs.t: Desert ecosystems - hot vs cold, adaptations

x: Low precipitation is common to hot and cold deserts; the Thar occurs in western Rajasthan and Kutch, while Ladakh and the Gobi are cold deserts.
Desert plants commonly have deep roots, small or spiny leaves and waxy cuticles.
Many desert animals are mostly nocturnal and possess water-saving adaptations.

secs.t: AP ecosystems - Kolleru, Pulicat, Coringa, Eastern Ghats

x: Kolleru is a freshwater lentic wetland located between the Godavari and Krishna deltas and is a Ramsar site.
Kolleru is the freshwater lake, Pulicat the brackish lagoon, Coringa the mangrove-estuary sanctuary and the Eastern Ghats the forest-to-thorn-forest transition region.
In the relevant AP region, dense tropical forests of the Eastern Ghats grade into thorn forests on the Rayalaseema plateau.

secs.t: Biomagnification vs bioaccumulation

x: Biomagnification is favoured by persistent, fat-soluble and non-biodegradable chemicals that become increasingly concentrated at higher trophic levels.
Biomagnification is the increase in toxin concentration at successively higher trophic levels, while bioaccumulation is build-up within a single organism.
DDT, methylmercury and toxic hydrocarbons from oil spills are all examples associated with accumulation or biomagnification in food chains and organisms.

secs.t: Food webs - complexity and stability

x: A food web consists of several interconnected food chains within an ecosystem.
A complex food web provides alternative pathways for energy and feeding relationships, increasing ecosystem stability.
Warming and ocean acidification
can cause coral bleaching and disrupt marine food chains.

secs.t: Limitations of ecological pyramids

x: Ecological pyramids assume a simple food chain and therefore do not adequately represent the complexity of food webs.
Ecological pyramids cannot place one species at two trophic levels, generally omit decomposers and may ignore organism size; counting organisms is also difficult.
Ecological pyramids do not display all interlinked food chains in complete detail; this is precisely one of the limitations arising from their simple food-chain assumption.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The newer ocean-carbon models incorporate
zooplankton grazing
as a process influencing the biological pump.
The study warned that thousands of alien plants may invade the warming
Arctic tundra
Nallamala and Seshachalam forests provide habitat for tigers, leopards, sloth bears and elephants.
Habitat is the address of an organism, niche is its profession or role, biome comprises many habitats, and ecosystem structure refers to what is present.
The Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve was notified in 2010, the corridors support major mammals, and the Chenchus are a PVTG living in the landscape.
The AP State Biodiversity Board is planning OECMs
outside protected areas
as part of broader conservation efforts.

rows.title: Biogeochemical cycles, ecological succession, ecosystem services
sub: Group-II M2-B-51: Biogeochemical cycles, ecological succession and ecosystem services

secs.t: Functions of environment and ecosystem services - resource supply, waste assimilation, life support, aesthetics, MEA categories

x: Exam angle: match function with description (waste decomposition = breakdown of organic waste into simpler compounds; cultural heritage = source of tradition).
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005, associated with the United Nations, classified ecosystem services as
provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting
services.
The Amazon estimate was about US$2.2–3.4 trillion, coral reefs about US$375 billion–9.9 trillion, and Costanza et al. estimated global ecosystem services at about US$33 trillion.
Costanza et al. estimated the annual value of global ecosystem services at approximately US$33 trillion in 1997.

secs.t: Ecological succession - primary vs secondary, pioneers on bare rock, sere, seral stages, phases, climax

x: Frederic Clements
first proposed the sequence of nudation, invasion, competition and co-action, reaction, and stabilisation in 1916.
Reaction
is the phase in which organisms modify environmental conditions such as soil, water, light and temperature, thereby facilitating later communities.
A newly formed volcanic island lacks a pre-existing community and soil, so its colonisation represents primary succession.
Hydrosere proceeds from phytoplankton through submerged and floating plants, reed-swamp, sedge-meadow, woodland and finally forest.
A xerosere on bare rock progresses from crustose lichens to foliose lichens, mosses, herbs and grasses, shrubs and finally a forest climax.
Pioneer communities colonise first, seral communities occupy intermediate stages, and the climax community is the stable terminal community related to the prevailing climate.

secs.t: Biogeochemical cycles - gaseous vs sedimentary, main reservoirs, CO2 sources and sinks, weathering-driven cycles

x: Without decomposers, dead organic matter is not effectively broken down, so nutrients remain locked in it and mineral movement is blocked.
Photosynthesis, ocean dissolution, carbonate sedimentation and silicate weathering all remove atmospheric carbon dioxide or store carbon for longer periods.
Phosphorus, sulphur and calcium
are sedimentary cycles whose principal reservoirs are soil and rocks in the Earth’s crust.

secs.t: Nitrogen fixation - legumes, root nodules, organisms by type, processes adding N to soil

x: Ammonification
is the conversion of organic nitrogen in dead matter into ammonia by decomposer bacteria and fungi.
Denitrification
removes nitrogen from soil by converting nitrate into atmospheric N2.
Rhizobium
is a symbiotic bacterium that fixes nitrogen in the root nodules of leguminous plants.
Blue-green algae such as Nostoc and Anabaena are cyanobacteria capable of nitrogen fixation in paddy fields.

secs.t: Water cycle regulation - forests and wetlands

x: Forests regulate water flow, conserve soil and moisture, recharge groundwater and moderate floods.
Both statements are true, and the storage, recharge and flow-regulation functions explain why wetlands are described as natural sponges.
Water carries elements through ecosystems.

secs.t: Succession types - hydrosere, xerosere, lithosere, psammosere

x: Xerosere begins on dry land and includes lithosere and psammosere; halosere begins on saline soil or water.
When sedge peat rises above the water level in a hydrosere,
alders and willows
invade the area.
Hydrosere ends in a wet woodland known as fen carr.
Lake sediments preserve a permanent record of ecological changes, making hydroseres better studied than xeroseres.

secs.t: Valuation - TEEB, natural capital accounting (EnviStats)

x: TEEB stands for
The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity
TEEB was launched in 2007 in the G8+5 context at Potsdam, hosted by UNEP, and aims to make the economic and other values of nature visible in decisions.
EnviStats India is an annual MoSPI compilation of environmental-economic accounts under the UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting framework.

secs.t: Human disruption of cycles - nitrogen overload, phosphorus runoff

x: Fossil-fuel burning raises CO2, and nitrogen and phosphorus runoff can cause algal blooms and eutrophication.

secs.t: Carbon cycle - sources, sinks, human alteration

x: Photosynthesis by plants, algae and some bacteria removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and incorporates carbon into organic matter.
Carbon is held in the atmosphere, oceans, forests and soils, while carbonate rocks and fossil fuels store carbon over long periods.
Both statements are true, and the release of stored carbon through fossil-fuel burning and deforestation explains the rise in atmospheric CO2 and associated climate change.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Energy is progressively lost, mainly as heat, but matter is reused through decomposers and biogeochemical cycles, helping ecosystems continue functioning.
Andhra Pradesh forests act as carbon sinks, regulate water flow and conserve soil and moisture, thereby providing important intangible ecosystem services.
Pricing nature can aid decision-making, but monetary valuation may undervalue cultural and spiritual services that are difficult to express in economic terms.

rows.title: Environmental issues and concerns - land degradation, desertification, deforestation, soil erosion
sub: Group-II M2-B-94: Other environmental challenges - desertification, land degradation and urban heat islands

secs.t: Deforestation - drivers, impacts, FAO Forest Resources Assessment data, zones with highest loss

x: Exam angle: fill-in-the-blank on FAO net-loss figures; check which FRA edition the question uses.
Deforestation removes vegetative cover, lowers soil-moisture retention, accelerates erosion and may lead to declining fertility and desertification.
The FRA 2025 figures record a decline in annual net forest loss from 10.7 million hectares in the 1990s to 4.12 million hectares per year during 2015–2025.
The highest forest loss is concentrated in tropical forests, especially in the Amazon, Congo Basin and Southeast Asia.

secs.t: Desertification and land degradation - semi-arid causes, DLD Atlas, extent

x: Desertification involves land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas due to climatic variation and human activity; it is not merely the spread of existing deserts.
The UNCCD Global Land Outlook estimates that land degradation costs more than
of global GDP through lost ecosystem services.
Overgrazing strips vegetation, deforestation exposes soil, water erosion removes topsoil and causes sedimentation, and wind erosion blows topsoil away in dry areas.

secs.t: Agriculture-driven degradation - modern agriculture, groundwater and topsoil depletion

x: The most conspicuous effects of modern agriculture are
soil degradation, pollution and ecological imbalance
Synthetic chemicals contaminate soil and water; over-irrigation with poor drainage causes waterlogging and salinity; and the projected affected share by 2050 is 50% of global arable land.
Soil Organic Carbon in Indian soils reportedly fell from
over 70 years.

secs.t: Forest and soil conservation movements → state and leader

x: The Chipko Movement began in 1973, the Mitti Bachao Abhiyan in 1977, and the Appiko Movement in 1983.
The Appiko Movement occurred in Karnataka in 1983 and was associated with Panduranga Hegde.
The Mitti Bachao Abhiyan began in Madhya Pradesh in the Tawa dam area of Hoshangabad in 1977 and opposed waterlogging and salinity.

secs.t: UNCCD - objectives, COP14 in India, LDN target year

x: The Global Land Outlook is the flagship publication of the UNCCD; editions mentioned include 2017 and 2022.
The correct sequence is Bonn Challenge in 2011, New York Declaration on Forests in 2014, India’s Paris pledge in 2015, and COP14 in 2019.
The World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought is observed on
17 June
, following a 1994 UNGA decision.

secs.t: Programmes - Aravalli Green Wall, watershed development, Soil Health Card

x: These programmes and approaches support soil assessment, agroforestry, and soil and water conservation.

secs.t: AP land degradation - Anantapur, Rayalaseema

x: All three figures are reported for Andhra Pradesh: desertification area up 3.45%, tree cover 2.87%, and forest cover 18.28%.
Fallow land covers 34.65 lakh hectares, equivalent to 21.26% of Andhra Pradesh, and exceeds the forest area.
Anantapur and Sri Sathya Sai are associated with drought-induced soil degradation, desertification, topsoil loss through wind erosion and groundwater depletion.

secs.t: Urban heat islands - causes, cool roofs, AP policy, Heat Action Plans

x: Air-conditioners cool indoor spaces but reject waste heat into the surrounding urban environment, thereby aggravating the urban heat island effect.
Cool roofs use white or reflective, high-reflectance coatings that reduce heat absorption and lower the indoor cooling load.
The Namo Van–Nagar Van Scheme promotes urban forests with the aim of reducing the urban heat island effect.

secs.t: Desertification geography and the Atlas

x: Africa, especially the Sahel region, and Asia are identified as the worst-hit regions in relation to desertification.
The Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas was published by ISRO's Space Applications Centre located at Ahmedabad.
Degraded land increased from 94.53 million hectares to
97.85 million hectares
between the two periods.
The share of degraded land rose from 28.8% during 2003–05 to 29.77% during 2018–19.

secs.t: Aravalli Green Wall, Great Green Wall, Bonn Challenge

x: The Aravalli Green Wall covers the Aravallis across
Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi
, acting as a barrier against the eastward spread of the Thar.
The Great Green Wall is an African Union-led belt across the Sahel, extending from Senegal to Djibouti, with a target of restoring 100 million hectares by 2030.

secs.t: Sand and dust storms, soil salinity

x: Sand and dust storms commonly affect drylands of north-western India, including Rajasthan, as well as West Asia and the Sahel.
The related day is observed on
12 July
, while 2025–2034 has been declared the UN Decade on Combating Sand and Dust Storms.
China's straw-checkerboard technique is used to fix shifting sand and stabilise dunes as part of desert-control efforts.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The cited figure is only
of the Union budget, which was presented as a reason for advocating a national environmental survey.
China's Three-North Protective Forest Program, also called the Great Green Wall of China, has checked desert spread but needs decades more to mature and achieve its broader objectives.

rows.title: Environmental legislation in India - Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981, Environment (Protection) Act 1986
sub: Group-II M2-B-79: Pollution control regulation - CPCB and SPCBs, the Water Act, Air Act and Environment (Protection) Act

secs.t: Environmental Acts - enactment chronology

x: Exam angle: arrange-in-order questions; Water (1974) always precedes Air (1981) and EPA (1986).
Exam angle: "arrange in chronological order" - Water 1974 → Water Cess 1977 → Forest 1980 → Air 1981 → EPA 1986 → NGT 2010.
The
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
, is described as India’s first pollution law and also created the pollution-control Boards.
The Forest Act requires prior Central approval for diversion, while the Air Act dates from 1981 and was amended in 1987 with stricter penalties.

secs.t: EPA 1986 - trigger, umbrella nature, powers, authorities, rules and notifications

x: The Central Government’s powers include prescribing emission and discharge standards, regulating industrial locations, managing hazardous wastes and protecting public health.
The Doon Valley notification of 1989 prohibited industries burning more than 24 metric tonnes of coal or fuel a day.
The CRZ notification of 1991 regulates coastal stretches and prohibits ash and waste dumping in the regulated areas.
The Dhanu Taluka notification of 1991 identified the area as ecologically fragile and prohibited power plants there.
The
EIA notification
, first issued in 1994 and revised in 2006, provides for prior environmental clearance.
Eco-Sensitive Zone notifications, the Plastic Waste Management Rules and the Green Credit Rules are all instruments notified under the Environment (Protection) Act.
The Green Credit Rules, 2023 provide
Green Credits
for voluntary tree planting on degraded land.
The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, in association with the Central Pollution Control Board, publishes standards in the Gazette.
The
Jan Vishwas Act, 2023
decriminalised the penalty regime under the Environment (Protection) Act.

secs.t: Air Act 1981 - purpose, noise, air pollution control areas

x: The principal objective of the Air Act is to prevent, control and abate air pollution and to maintain prescribed air-quality standards.
The State Government
may declare an air pollution control area under Chapter IV, particularly Sections 19 to 31, of the Air Act.
Section 31A empowers the pollution control authorities to issue directions, including directions connected with enforcement and environmental compensation.
The Water Act deals with effluent-discharge standards; the Air Act deals with air-control areas and emissions; the Cess Act funds the Boards; and the 1987 amendment added noise.

secs.t: Water Act 1974 - purpose, boards, consent, Cess Act link

x: The
Central Board for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution
, created in 1974, was renamed the CPCB by the 1988 amendment.
The Water Cess Act provided a 25 per cent rebate for installing treatment plants, encouraging reduction and treatment of polluted discharges.
The Cess Act had 17 sections, its proceeds went to the Consolidated Fund of India, and it was subsumed or repealed with the GST framework in 2017.

secs.t: Jan Vishwas Act 2023 - decriminalised environmental provisions

x: The PLI Act mentioned in this context is the
Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991
, which was amended by the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023.
The Central Government may provide Environmental Relief Fund money to the Central Pollution Control Board and State Pollution Control Boards for restoration.
The
penalty rates were shifted to rules
, while the amendment also replaced specified criminal consequences with penalties.

secs.t: Environment-related cases in news - M.C. Mehta, Vellore and others

x: The National Green Tribunal issued the suo motu notice to
Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh
regarding sewage entering drinking water.

The Vanashakti ruling dealt with ex post facto clearances, the NGT notice concerned sewage contamination of drinking water in three States, and integrated consent with indefinite CTO validity was a reported January 2026 development.

secs.t: CPCB and SPCBs - setting up, law, functions, enforcement, chairperson

x: The Air Act, 1981
added air pollution functions to the CPCB, which had originally been constituted under the Water Act.
SPCBs inspect plants, analyse samples, grant consents and enforce pollution standards within their jurisdiction.
In March 2026, the NAMP network comprised
1,646 stations in 603 cities
NCAP targets a
reduction in PM10 by 2025-26 compared with the 2019-20 baseline.

secs.t: AP Pollution Control Board - head office, functions, online consent, compensation

x: The APPCB implements the Water Act, Air Act and Environment (Protection) Act, along with rules relating to hazardous, biomedical, plastic and solid waste.
The APPCB issues siting guidelines for industries and also prepares SOPs for marine outfall monitoring and hazardous waste.
The APPCB levies environmental compensation under
Section 33A of the Water Act and Section 31A of the Air Act
; the power was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2025.

secs.t: MoEF/MoEFCC - establishment, renaming, attached bodies

x: The Department of Environment was established in 1980, became the Ministry of Environment and Forests in 1985, and was renamed MoEFCC in 2014.
The Forest Survey of India is among the bodies under the Ministry.

secs.t: Consent mechanism - CTE/CTO, colour categories

x: CTO is valid
until cancelled
under the amended mechanism, replacing the earlier periodic-renewal approach.
The White category covers industries with a CPCB score of 20 or less and is described as practically non-polluting, requiring no consent or environmental clearance.
The January 2026 reform provides for a single application for Air and Water consents plus waste authorisations, while consent to operate remains valid until cancelled.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Water Act of 1974 is regarded as India’s first pollution-control law, while the National Green Tribunal Act of 2010 is the latest in the stated legislative chain.
NCAP targets an improvement of up to
in PM10 concentration by 2025–26 in 130 cities, using 2019–20 as the baseline year.
APPCB was established in 1976 under the Water Act, enforces the major environmental laws and waste rules, and provides industrial siting guidelines.

rows.title: Environmental Impact Assessment - process, EIA notification, public hearing, criticism
sub: Group-II M2-B-80: Environmental Impact Assessment and the National Green Tribunal

secs.t: Post-facto clearance and exemption cases - Vanashakti, Noble M. Paikada, Common Cause, Alembic

x: Exam angle: "primary issue in case X" - match case to the exemption or post-facto question it decided.
Exam angle: prior EC is mandatory under EIA 2006; post-facto approval only as a narrow exception.
Noble M. Paikada v. Union of India examined the 2020 exemption from environmental clearance for
extraction of ordinary earth for linear projects
The May 2025 Vanashakti ruling characterised retrospective environmental clearances as
a gross illegality and an anathema to environmental law

The May 2025 ruling struck down the specified instruments, was recalled in November 2025 by a 2:1 majority, relied on the cited earlier cases, and affected projects valued at approximately ₹20,000 crore.

secs.t: EIA vs related tools - SEA, LCA, Cumulative Impact Assessment, environmental audit

x: EIA concerns a project before it starts; LCA covers a product or process through its life cycle; cumulative impact assessment examines combined effects; and an environmental audit checks an operating unit after the fact.
Sector-wide EIAs are intended to incorporate strategic and cumulative perspectives, allowing impacts across a sector or region to be assessed rather than examining projects in isolation.

secs.t: Cleaner production and green chemistry - principles and link to assessment

x: Cleaner production is preventive: it reduces waste and pollution at source through measures such as process change and input substitution, rather than relying mainly on end-of-pipe treatment.
The twelve principles of green chemistry are associated with Paul Anastas and John Warner and were formulated in 1998.
Cleaner production and green chemistry reduce impacts during design, so EIA and LCA identify fewer residual impacts that require mitigation.

secs.t: EIA process - screening to monitoring

x: Screening
determines whether EIA is required and identifies the applicable project category.
Scoping identifies the key environmental issues and establishes the Terms of Reference for the EIA study.
Baseline environmental conditions are surveyed, alternatives are compared during impact prediction, and mitigation planning includes an Environmental Management Plan.
During appraisal, the relevant expert committee evaluates the EIA report.

secs.t: EIA Notifications 1994 and 2006 - categories A/B, EAC, SEIAA

x: The Draft EIA 2020 proposed post-facto clearance upon payment of penalties and a shorter public consultation period.
The backup bodies are
SAEIA and SCEIA
, which step in when a State’s SEIAA or SEAC lapses.
Category A projects do not undergo screening; they always require full EIA, are appraised by EAC and cleared by MoEFCC.
MoEFCC had earlier proposed the Standing Committee on EIA and the Standing Authority on EIA, abbreviated
SCEIA and SAEIA
The
AP State Environment Impact Assessment Authority
(AP SEIAA) clears Category B projects in Andhra Pradesh under the EIA Notification, 2006.

secs.t: Draft EIA Notification 2020 - contested provisions

x: The draft proposed post-facto environmental clearance through appraisal, penalties, compensation and remediation plans.
The draft proposed a 20-day notice period, more B2 or exempt projects and yearly compliance reports.
The 2020 draft was not finalised and was contested, particularly for proposing post-facto clearance and shorter consultation periods.

secs.t: Public hearing - exempted projects, notice period

x: Public consultation is
a mandatory two-fold process
involving public hearing and written responses for scheduled projects.
The State Pollution Control Board conducts the hearing, while
the District Collector
presides over it.
Defence, national-security and strategic projects
may be exempt because their details are kept confidential.
B2 projects and units located inside notified industrial estates are among the stated exemptions from public hearing.

secs.t: PARIVESH portal - single-window clearances

x: PARIVESH is an online single-window platform for environment, forest, wildlife and Coastal Regulation Zone clearances.
The PARIVESH portal was launched in 2018.
PARIVESH expands to
Pro-Active and Responsive facilitation by Interactive, Virtuous and Environmental Single-window Hub
PARIVESH is used for the 120-day escalation process to the Standing Committee on Environmental Impact Assessment.

secs.t: EIA history - NEPA origin, first sectors in India

x: India's EIA process began in
when the Planning Commission asked DST to examine river-valley projects.
Large public-sector projects requiring
Public Investment Board
clearance became another early area of EIA application.
2011 concerned river-valley projects in specific contexts; 2012/2018 concerned mining and mining/infrastructure; 2013 concerned thermal power; and 2015 concerned expansion and modernisation.

secs.t: Landmark NGT orders - mining bans, plantation/penalty directions, fines on states, AP cases

x: NGT directions and matters include Ganga pollution control, waste management, industrial monitoring, and cases such as the Dhanauri wetland and Saparnika river matters.
Following the Visakhapatnam styrene leak in May 2020, the NGT took suo motu cognisance and ordered an interim deposit of Rs 50 crore.
A High-Powered Committee was set up on the directions of the
National Green Tribunal
in relation to the Great Nicobar project.

secs.t: Clearance and inter-state disputes over AP projects - Polavaram, Amaravati

x: The Polavaram inter-state dispute concerns submergence in neighbouring
Odisha and Chhattisgarh
and was raised before the Supreme Court.

secs.t: Clearance bodies - EAC, SEIAA, PARIVESH

x: Under the stated 2026 arrangement, a proposal is auto-transferred through PARIVESH if the SEAC does not appraise it within
120 days
The stated backup bodies are SAEIA in place of SEIAA and SCEIA in place of SEAC.
The tenure was raised to
four years, with a maximum of two terms and an age limit of 70
years for members of SEIAA, EAC and SEAC.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All four statements describe identified criticisms of the EIA process: proponent-paid consultants, absence of a central baseline data bank, weak emergency plans and exemptions from hearings.
Telangana sought Supreme Court review of the Polavaram EIA, while the APPCB hearing on the Prakasam Barrage water aerodrome drew criticism from the Human Rights Forum for an error-ridden draft EIA.

rows.title: Environmental institutions - MoEFCC, CPCB and SPCBs, National Green Tribunal, National Biodiversity Authority

secs.t: National Green Tribunal - Act, benches, purpose, composition, jurisdiction, NGT vs CPCB

x: Exam angle: bench-to-city matching; "which Act is NOT under NGT" (Wildlife Act).
Exam angle: APPSC 2018 asked for the date it was set up (
18 October 2010
). APPSC 2025 asked its purpose (environmental and pollution-control cases).
The Principal Bench is at New Delhi; Pune is a zonal bench location; and Jodhpur and Shillong are circuit bench locations.
The right to a healthy environment is read into the right to life under
Article 21
of the Constitution, and the NGT helps enforce this environmental right.
The NGT is not bound by the CPC, follows natural justice, has civil-court powers, and is expected to dispose of cases within six months.

secs.t: CPCB - setup, parent Act, chairman, functions, NAMP

x: The Air Act added air-related functions, the Environment Protection Act widened its scope, and the CPCB functions as a statutory body under MoEFCC.
CAAQMS
refers to the continuous ambient air quality monitoring system used for real-time air monitoring.
The CPCB coordinates SPCBs, provides technical help, supports research and training, and performs monitoring and regulatory functions.

secs.t: SPCBs - APPCB, labs, enforcement, consents

x: Consent to Operate
is required before production or discharge begins.
All four statements describe stated APPCB responsibilities, including enforcement, waste-management rules, siting guidance, SOPs and cleaner production.
The APPCB uses computerised inspection in connection with
Ease of Doing Business
initiatives.
The APPCB was established in 1976 by the
Government of Andhra Pradesh under the Water Act, 1974

secs.t: NGT predecessors - NET Act 1995, NEAA

x: The Act was never operationalised, was repealed by the NGT Act, and provided for strict liability in hazardous-substance accidents.
The National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995 provided for strict liability in cases of damage resulting from hazardous-substance accidents.
The NGT combines original jurisdiction over environmental disputes with the appellate role earlier performed by the NEAA.

secs.t: MoEFCC - origin, formation, renaming

x: The correct sequence is Department of Environment in 1980, Air Act in 1981, Ministry of Environment and Forests in 1985, and MoEFCC renaming in 2014.
All three statements are correct according to the stated current information: the allocation is 0.07%, MoEFCC is nodal for India’s NR7 biodiversity report, and it runs Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan.

secs.t: Environmental research institutes → location

x: The Wildlife Institute of India is at Dehradun, the Botanical Survey of India is at Kolkata and GBPNIHE is at Kosi-Katarmal, Almora.
SACON is located at Coimbatore, IITR at Lucknow, CMLRE at Kochi and ZSI at Kolkata.
ENVIS is the MoEFCC’s network of environmental-information centres and is now known as EIACP.

secs.t: National Biodiversity Authority - HQ, year, biopiracy, three tiers, APSBB

x: Foreigners require NBA approval to access bio-resources or associated traditional knowledge, and such approval precedes the grant of intellectual property rights.
The City Biodiversity Index, biodiversity parks on the flood plains of five polluted rivers and the Gloriosa superba cultivation pilot are APSBB initiatives.
Foreign access to bio-resources or associated traditional knowledge requires NBA approval, and benefit-sharing with local communities is part of the framework.

secs.t: Other statutory bodies - CAQM, CGWA, NMCG

x: The
Commission for Air Quality Management
(CAQM), established under the CAQM Act, 2021, replaced EPCA in the NCR and adjoining areas.
NMCG is the successor set-up to the National Ganga River Basin Authority (
NGRBA
), which was established in 2009 under the Environment (Protection) Act.
The National River Conservation Plan covers pollution abatement in
38 rivers in 16 States outside the Ganga basin

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The NGT directed southern States and Puducherry to execute action plans under the
National Clean Air Programme
(NCAP).
Approximately
of the expenditure under the referred NCAP action plans went towards road dust.
The Environmental (Protection) Fund Rules, 2026 provide for financing CPCB and State Pollution Control Boards.
Guntur stood second in the
towns category
of Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan 2026, which covered 130 cities.

rows.title: International environmental treaties - Stockholm 1972, Rio 1992, Ramsar, CITES, CBD and its protocols
sub: Group-II M2-B-58: Recent plans and targets - Convention on Biological Diversity, Nagoya and Cartagena Protocols
Group-II M2-B-59: Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and India's biodiversity targets
Group-II M2-B-60: Wildlife conservation - CITES: structure, appendices and species listings relevant to India

secs.t: Rio Earth Summit 1992 - name, venue, documents, Rio+5, Rio+20

x: Exam angle: "Agenda 21 / Rio Declaration came from which summit" - Earth Summit 1992.
Exam angle: match conference with year and output
Rio+20, held in Rio de Janeiro in 2012, produced “The Future We Want”, launched the Sustainable Development Goal process and was associated with the High-Level Political Forum.
World Environment Day is linked to UNEP, World Refugee Day to UNHCR, International Day of Yoga to the UN General Assembly, and World Food Day to FAO.

secs.t: CBD protocols and targets - Cartagena, Nagoya, Aichi, Kunming-Montreal

x: Cartagena concerns biosafety, Nagoya concerns access and benefit-sharing, the Aichi Targets numbered 20 for 2011–2020, and the Kunming-Montreal GBF contains four 2050 goals and 23 targets for 2030.
The framework seeks to cut harmful subsidies by 500 billion dollars annually and also aims to restore 30 per cent of degraded ecosystems.
COP-15 began in Kunming in 2021 and concluded in Montreal in December 2022, producing the Kunming-Montreal GBF.
COP-15 also functioned as the 10th MOP of Cartagena and the 4th MOP of Nagoya, and it was associated with the GBF Fund under the GEF.
CBD COP-16 was held at Cali, Colombia, in October–November 2024 and resumed at Rome in February 2025.
The Nagoya Protocol establishes the framework for access and fair benefit-sharing arising from the utilisation of genetic resources.
India’s first National Report on the Nagoya Protocol recorded approximately
2.76 lakh
Biodiversity Management Committees.

secs.t: Stockholm Conference 1972 - name, venue, outcomes, India

x: The Stockholm Conference produced the 26-principle Stockholm Declaration and an Action Plan, led to the establishment of UNEP and resulted in 5 June being observed as World Environment Day.
The 1972 Stockholm Conference was the UN Conference on the Human Environment, while the 1992 Rio Summit was UNCED, focused on environment and development.

secs.t: CITES - other name, appendices, secretariat, TRAFFIC

x: CITES was adopted on 3 March 1973, entered into force on 1 July 1975, and has a UNEP-administered Secretariat in Geneva.
CoP19 in 2022 moved
54 shark and ray species
to CITES Appendix II.
CITES prohibits commercial trade for approximately 3 per cent of the species covered and regulates the remaining 97 per cent; the statement reverses these proportions.
The CITES Trade Database is maintained by the United Nations Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre (
UNEP-WCMC

secs.t: CMS - appendices, COP hosted by India

x: CMS Appendix I contains endangered migratory species requiring strict protection.
CMS Appendix II covers migratory species whose conservation requires international cooperation agreements.
CMS COP-13 was hosted at Gandhinagar, India, in February 2020.
The
Great Indian Bustard, Asian elephant and Bengal florican
were added to CMS Appendix I at COP-13.

secs.t: Environment days → date

x: International Day for Biological Diversity is observed annually on
22 May
World Environment Day on 5 June commemorates the opening of the
Stockholm Conference

secs.t: Ramsar Convention - year, obligations, Montreux Record, India's sites, AP

x: The Ramsar Convention Secretariat is located at
Gland, Switzerland
Chilika Lake
was the first Indian Ramsar site, designated in 1981.
Udaipur and Indore became India's first accredited Wetland Cities in January 2025.
The resolution was adopted at COP-15 on 30 July 2025, and the Amrit Dharohar strategy dates to June 2023.
The
Wetlands Rules, 2017
constitute the domestic legal framework specified for wetlands.

secs.t: Treaty → secretariat, year, India's status

x: India hosted UNCCD COP-14 in 2019, ratified the World Heritage Convention in 1977 and is a member of the IWC.
The Montreal Protocol was adopted at Montreal in 1987, its Ozone Secretariat is at Nairobi, and India is a Party.
UNCCD COP-17 is hosted by
Mongolia
and has the theme “Restoring Land.

secs.t: High Seas Treaty (BBNJ) - status, India

x: India signed the BBNJ Agreement in
September 2024
; the agreement later entered into force on 17 January 2026.

secs.t: Nagoya Protocol - subject, utilisation, benefit-sharing, entry into force, India's law

x: Its full name is the
Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization
The Nagoya Protocol is a legally binding supplementary agreement to the Convention on Biological Diversity; it is not merely voluntary.
The pillars are prior informed consent, Mutually Agreed Terms for benefit-sharing, and compliance against illegal acquisition.

secs.t: UN biodiversity observances
Cartagena Protocol - subject, AIA, BCH, Indian ministry

x: The Cartagena Protocol deals with the safe transfer, handling and use of
Living Modified Organisms resulting from modern biotechnology
Under AIA, the importing country must be informed and must consent before the first transboundary movement of a Living Modified Organism.
MoEF&CC is India's nodal ministry, and the
Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee
handles approvals for genetically engineered organisms.

secs.t: Protocols - parent convention

x: The Nagoya Protocol is a protocol under the Convention on Biological Diversity.
The Nagoya-Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol on Liability and Redress is supplementary to the
Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety
and is therefore connected to the CBD framework.

secs.t: CBD implementation in India - NBA, SBBs, BMCs, AP Board

x: BMCs support Nagoya objectives, can levy collection fees for access to bio-resources in their area, and prepare People's Biodiversity Registers.
ABS has mobilised over Rs 266 crore since 2008; Red Sanders contributed 45%, amounting to about Rs 120 crore, while seeds contributed 32.3%.
The AP State Biodiversity Board constitutes BMCs, prepares PBRs, processes ABS applications and performs several biodiversity-related functions.
The objectives mirror the CBD: conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components and fair sharing of benefits.

secs.t: Aichi Biodiversity Targets - number, goals, status

x: The 20 Aichi Biodiversity Targets were adopted at CBD COP10, held at Nagoya in 2010.
The five broad goals included addressing underlying causes, reducing direct pressures, safeguarding ecosystems and species, enhancing benefits, and participatory implementation.
The status assessment identified weak buy-in beyond
environment ministries
as one of the implementation problems.

secs.t: Headline targets - 30x30, restoration, invasives, harmful subsidies, pesticides and nutrients

x: Target 2 calls for effective
restoration of 30% of degraded land and water ecosystems
Target 6 seeks at least a
50 percent
reduction in the introduction and establishment of invasive alien species by 2030.
Target 7 covers both excess nutrient losses and overall pesticide risk, with each to be halved.

secs.t: KMGBF - adopting COP, goals, targets, deadline

x: The KMGBF was adopted at CBD COP15 in Montreal in December 2022.
Goal A
addresses extinction by seeking a tenfold reduction in extinction rate and risk and a halt to human-induced extinction.
Goal D concerns adequate finance and technology and refers to closing the
US$700 billion
per year biodiversity-finance gap.

secs.t: Biodiversity finance - GBF Fund, resource mobilisation, Cali Fund

x: The Global Biodiversity Framework Fund is set up under the
Global Environment Facility
Target 19 seeks at least
US$200 billion
per year by 2030 from all sources.
The Cali Fund was associated with COP16 at Cali in October 2024 and addresses benefit-sharing from DSI use, with the stated contribution expectations for large users.

secs.t: India's updated NBSAP - national targets, submission

x: India’s updated NBSAP contains
23 national targets
matching the 23 targets of the KMGBF.
India released its updated NBSAP at COP16 in Cali in October 2024.
Target 13 of India’s updated NBSAP concerns
access and benefit-sharing

secs.t: Monitoring framework - headline indicators, national reports, COP16 outcomes

x: Progress is tracked through
headline indicators
of the KMGBF monitoring framework.
COP16 at Cali, resumed at Rome, was associated with the Cali Fund for DSI, implementation of the KMGBF including 30x30, and a permanent subsidiary body on Indigenous peoples under Article 8(j).
COP16 was held initially at Cali in October 2024 and resumed at
Rome in February 2025

secs.t: Indigenous peoples and local communities

x: Implementation of 30x30 is to respect indigenous territories.
Target 22 secures the full participation and rights of indigenous peoples and local communities over lands and resources.
India’s route includes
Biodiversity Management Committees, People’s Biodiversity Registers and access and benefit-sharing
mechanisms to connect conservation benefits with local and tribal communities.

secs.t: Wildlife conventions and bodies - mandate and legal status

x: CMS is also called the Bonn Convention, focuses on migratory species and is a binding treaty under UNEP.
TRAFFIC is an NGO network of WWF and IUCN that works to ensure wildlife trade does not become a threat to conservation.
CMS is the Bonn Convention, has its UNEP-linked Secretariat at Bonn, and India has been a Party since 1983.

secs.t: India's accession and implementing law

x: Schedule IV is the CITES schedule; invasive alien species are regulated under a separate new section, not through the CITES schedule.
The Zoological Survey of India hosts a CITES Cell and is an authorised wildlife-forensic body.
In 2025, the Zoological Survey of India analysed 1,545 confiscated specimens belonging to 105 species.

secs.t: Appendices I, II, III - criteria and trade

x: Appendix II includes species that are not necessarily threatened with extinction but could become so without effective trade controls.
Appendix III
is used for species protected in at least one country that seeks assistance from other countries.
The walrus is an example associated with Appendix III, where Canada’s protection and request for cooperation are relevant.

secs.t: Indian species in CITES appendices

x: The Indian star tortoise was uplisted to Appendix I on India’s proposal at
CoP18 in 2019
The Indian and Chinese pangolins are in Appendix I, and over 500,000 pangolins were seized globally during 2016–2024.
India proposed changes concerning
rosewood, otters, tortoises, Tokay gecko and wedgefish

secs.t: Red sanders of Seshachalam (AP) - CITES and RST

x: Pterocarpus santalinus is endemic to the Seshachalam and southern Eastern Ghats and is classified as Endangered by IUCN.
Red sanders is smuggled largely because of demand in
China and Japan
Red sanders contributes
of India’s ABS income, stated as Rs 120 crore.
The Red Sanders Protection Scheme covers 5,300.97 sq km across
seven districts

secs.t: Wildlife Crime Control Bureau - CITES enforcement

x: WCCB is a statutory body under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
WCCB was set up in 2007 under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, following the 2006 amendment.
WCCB assists Customs and builds the wildlife-crime database.
ICCWC links CITES with INTERPOL, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the World Customs Organization.
MIKE tracks elephant poaching.

secs.t: CITES COP - frequency, recent venue, India's proposals

x: CoP3 was held in 1981, CoP18 in 2019, CoP19 in 2022 and CoP20 in 2025.
CoP20 was held at Samarkand in 2025, marked 50 years of CITES and added 77 species.
At CoP20, India defeated the European Union proposal for a stricter listing of Guggul, scientifically known as Commiphora wightii.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: UNFCCC, CBD and UNCCD are the three Rio Conventions addressing climate, biodiversity and land-related concerns respectively.
The Ramsar Convention dates from 1971, the Stockholm Conference from 1972 and the Rio Earth Summit from 1992.
The amendment has been criticised for diluting access and benefit-sharing, increasing biopiracy risks and reducing the role of local communities.
CMS COP15 in Campo Grande, Brazil
, launched the Global Initiative on the Taking of Migratory Species.
Whale shark, oceanic whitetip shark and manta rays
were uplisted to CITES Appendix I at CoP20.
Red sanders connects international trade regulation under CITES, its IUCN Endangered status, smuggling in Andhra Pradesh and access-and-benefit-sharing income.

rows.title: Sustainable development - meaning, nature, scope and components
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-72

secs.t: Sustainable development summits - venue, formal UN name, outcome documents

x: The 2012 UNCSD at Rio de Janeiro was known as Rio+20, adopted The Future We Want and decided to frame the SDGs.
Rio+20 in 2012 produced ‘The Future We Want’, initiated the SDG process and established the UNEA with universal membership.
The First Five Year Plan belongs to 1951–56, the Millennium Declaration to 2000, Rio+20 to 2012 and Agenda 2030 adoption to 2015.

secs.t: Pillars of sustainable development - number, names, odd-one-out, triple bottom line

x: Economic development, social equity and environmental protection are interlinked pillars that must be balanced rather than pursued in isolation.
The triple bottom line is commonly expressed as
People, Planet and Profit
, corresponding broadly to social, environmental and economic concerns.

secs.t: Goals and principles - intergenerational equity, precautionary, polluter pays, carrying capacity

x: The precautionary principle states that lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone cost-effective preventive measures, making statement 2 false.
CBDR recognises shared responsibility while assigning greater duties to developed nations in view of their capacities and historical contribution.
Carrying capacity refers to the level of human use that ecosystems can support without losing their ability to function and regenerate.

secs.t: Scope statements - what the concept includes and excludes; resource use by the present generation

x: Sustainable development includes meeting present needs, equity within and across generations, and inclusion.
Leave no one behind expresses the commitment to inclusion and equity in development outcomes.
The National Environment Policy, 2006 holds that conservation and livelihood security are linked rather than opposed.

secs.t: Measures - Green GDP, GPI, ecological footprint, Earth Overshoot Day

x: An ecological footprint estimates the productive land and sea area required to supply consumption and absorb generated wastes, expressed in global hectares.
Earth Overshoot Day marks the point in a year when humanity's demand on ecological resources exceeds Earth's regenerative capacity for that year.
The Sustainable Development Report and its SDG Index are associated with UN SDSN, whereas NITI Aayog's SDG India Index ranks Indian States.

secs.t: Judicial recognition in India - landmark cases

x: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India
(1996) recognised sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle in Indian environmental law.
The NGT benches mentioned are at Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai.
The NGT applies all three principles: sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.

secs.t: Swarna Andhra @2047 vision - sustainability components

x: The Swarna Andhra @2047 vision is aligned with
Viksit Bharat @2047
Sustainability and Climate Resilience
is one of the strategic pillars of Swarna Andhra @2047.
The July 2026 AP-UN-Habitat MoU envisages a Centre of Excellence for Urban Affairs in
Amaravati
The MoU covers climate-resilient cities, is connected with SDG 11, and provides for a Centre of Excellence for Urban Affairs in Amaravati.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The most frequently asked themes are Stockholm, Rio, the Brundtland Commission and the Sustainable Development Goals.
APFDC is cited as a sustainability model involving
49,743 hectares of plantations
The first Earth Summit was held at Rio in 1992, while the first definition is associated with the Brundtland Commission in 1987.

sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-72

secs.t: 17 SDGs - goal number to theme, number of targets, adoption summit, deadline

x: Exam angle: "How many targets?" answer
; "Goal 4?" answer
Quality Education
; "Goal 5?" answer
Gender Equality
SDG 4 concerns quality education, SDG 7 affordable and clean energy, SDG 12 responsible consumption and production, and SDG 16 peace, justice and strong institutions.
The SDGs were adopted in the document titled “
Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development

secs.t: Nature of Agenda 2030 - universal applicability, human-rights basis, origin of the proposal

x: Agenda 2030 is guided by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948, together with international human-rights treaties.
The Rio+20 outcome document titled “
The Future We Want
” called for global goals to follow the MDGs.
The
Universal Declaration of Human Rights
, along with international human-rights treaties, guides the Agenda 2030 framework.

secs.t: SDG to Indian scheme matching (SDG 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 11, 13)

x: SDG 1 is associated with MGNREGA, SDG 2 with the National Food Security Act, SDG 3 with Ayushman Bharat and SDG 4 with Samagra Shiksha.
SDG 5 matches Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, SDG 6 Jal Jeevan Mission, SDG 7 Saubhagya and SDG 11 Smart Cities Mission.
India’s National Action Plan on Climate Change, comprising eight missions, is associated with SDG 13.

secs.t: Goal-specific statements - Goal 4, Goal 5, Goal 10

x: Goal 4 includes
affordable technical, vocational and tertiary education
, along with equitable schooling, early-childhood care and literacy.
All four statements describe areas covered by SDG 5, Gender Equality.
A
universal compulsory gold-backed currency
is not identified as an SDG 10 reform.
One of the SDG 10-related measures is to reduce remittance costs below
3 percent

secs.t: Chronology of development milestones
Sustainable Development Report and MoSPI SDG-NIF progress reports

x: The Sustainable Development Report is published by the
United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network
(SDSN).
India was ranked 99th out of 167 countries in the 2025 Sustainable Development Report, with a score of about 67.
India ranked below Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka; therefore, it did not rank above all its South Asian neighbours.
The SDG-NIF Progress Report 2026 contains 277 indicators covering all 17 SDGs.

secs.t: SDGs vs MDGs

x: The MDGs mainly focused on developing countries, while the SDGs are universal in scope.
The SDGs have a broader social, economic and environmental focus and are guided by the principle of leaving no one behind.
The maternal mortality ratio fell by
45 percent
during the period associated with the MDGs.

secs.t: SDG localisation - NER District SDG Index, LSDGs in Gram Panchayats, AP

x: The NER District SDG Index is associated with NITI Aayog and the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (MoDoNER), with support from UNDP.
Nagaland
recorded the widest inter-district spread, at 15.07 points.
The Ministry of Panchayati Raj framework groups the localised SDGs into nine themes.
Alluri Sitharama Raju (ASR) district ranked first on the Basic Infrastructure theme in the March 2026 ranking.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Current relevance:
India reached its best-ever SDR rank of
94th
in 2026, and MoSPI's NIF Progress Report 2026 tracks
277 indicators
AP angle:
74, Front Runner, 9th, with SDG 7 at rank 1.

rows.title: Sustainable development in practice - green economy, circular economy and ESG
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-72

secs.t: Circular economy - principles, linear vs circular, action plans

x: NITI Aayog and MoEFCC committees drew up action plans for priority streams including
plastics, e-waste, batteries, tyres and metals
The EPR frameworks are reported to have recycled 308 lakh tonnes of plastic, e-waste and batteries and generated 296.53 lakh tonnes of EPR certificates.
AMRUT 2.0 aims to reuse treated water for 20% of city demand and 40% of industrial demand.

secs.t: Green economy and green technology - meaning, features

x: A green economy reduces environmental risks and ecological scarcity, decouples growth from resource use and pollution, and fosters green industries and green jobs.
High cost is a major barrier to green technology, particularly for developing countries; it is not necessarily inexpensive.
The Green Hydrogen Mission has an outlay of Rs 19,744 crore, targets 5 MMT annually and is linked with the net-zero target for 2070.

secs.t: International initiatives - European Green Deal, UNEP GEI, PAGE

x: The European Green Deal aims at a climate-neutral EU by 2050 and at least a 55% reduction in greenhouse gases by 2030 compared with 1990.

Farm to Fork concerns a sustainable food system; the Circular Economy Action Plan concerns resource efficiency and recycling; the Biodiversity Strategy protects and restores ecosystems; and the Just Transition Fund supports affected regions.

secs.t: Green Skill Development Programme

x: The Green Skill Development Programme was launched in 2017 by the
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
The programme was built on the
ENVIS network
The programme trains youth in biodiversity conservation, pollution monitoring, waste management, forestry, wildlife and allied environmental sectors.

secs.t: Green Chemistry and Cleaner Production - principles, link with EIA and LCA

x: Paul Anastas and John Warner
introduced the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry in 1998.

Green chemistry and cleaner production minimise waste and pollution and promote sustainability throughout the product life cycle, supporting the objectives of Environmental Impact Assessment and Life-Cycle Assessment.
Green Pharmacy applies green chemistry to the
design, use and disposal of medicines

secs.t: Greenwashing

x: Greenwashing is the practice of making false or exaggerated environmental claims about a product, firm or investment.
A clear taxonomy helps regulators identify and curb greenwashing as well as transition washing.

secs.t: Green finance - bonds, green deposits, climate finance taxonomy

x: The European Investment Bank pioneered green bonds in 2007, followed by the World Bank in 2008, and the proceeds support environment-friendly projects.
The Sovereign Green Bonds were announced in Budget 2022–23, their framework was issued in 2022, and the first issue in 2023 amounted to Rs 8,000 crore.
India's first blue bond is planned through Sagarmala Finance Corporation Ltd for Rs 1,000 crore in FY 2026–27.

secs.t: ESG - pillars, BRSR, ratings

x: ESG stands for
Environmental, Social and Governance
, which are its three pillars.
SEBI
regulates ESG Rating Providers in India.
Public financial institutions publish Green Bond Frameworks and ESG financing policies, and they carry ESG impact ratings.

secs.t: Resource efficiency - Draft NREP, EPR, Green Credit Programme

x: The Draft National Resource Efficiency Policy promotes secondary raw materials and proposes a National Resource Efficiency Authority.
The Green Credit Programme is
a market-based incentive for voluntary environmental actions
such as tree plantation and water conservation.
The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme is stated to be scheduled for being put into operation; it is distinct from the Green Credit Programme.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Andhra Pradesh has the Reuse of Treated Used Water Policy 2026, includes an Electric Mobility Policy in its 2024–29 policy suite, and is among the states that digitised clearances under BRAP.
Without a final green taxonomy, the classification of genuinely green activities may be unclear, increasing the risk of
greenwashing

rows.title: International treaties on chemicals and waste - Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm POPs, Minamata; Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment
sub: Group-II M2-B-92: Ozone layer depletion - causes, ozone hole, effects; Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment

secs.t: Ozone depletion science - ODS, ozone hole, UV effects, unit

x: Exam angle: "which gas causes ozone depletion", ODS matched to its use, assertion-reason on CFCs.
UV-B exposure can cause DNA damage, skin cancer, eye cataracts and suppression of the human immune system.
UV radiation releases chlorine and bromine atoms, which catalytically destroy ozone.
Their use in appliances and aerosols does not explain their greenhouse effect and ozone-depleting action; those arise from their atmospheric chemical properties.
HCFCs
were introduced as transitional CFC substitutes, but they still deplete ozone, though generally less strongly than CFCs.
CFCs are associated with refrigeration and aerosols; halons with fire extinguishers; methyl bromide with fumigation; and HCFCs with transitional substitution.

secs.t: Montreal Protocol - year, focus, ODS, universal ratification, India's HCFC plan

x: The Protocol covers approximately 100 man-made ozone-depleting chemicals, including CFCs, halons, HCFCs and methyl bromide.
The Protocol was adopted at Montreal, Canada, and is regarded as the first and only UN treaty universally ratified, with 198 Parties in the stated current account.
The Multilateral Fund supports developing countries through technical and financial assistance for implementing ODS phase-out obligations.
The Protocol is estimated to avoid approximately
of warming by 2050 because many ODS are also potent greenhouse gases.
The dates are 1 January 2001 for halons, 2003 for CFCs in manufacturing, 2010 for CTC, methyl chloroform and CFCs in MDIs, and 2015 for methyl bromide.
Under Stage-II, India became the first developing country to fully phase out HCFC-141b in rigid foam, achieving a 44 percent reduction against the 35 percent target by January 2020.
The Vienna Convention was adopted in 1985, the Montreal Protocol in 1987, the Multilateral Fund in 1991, and the Kigali Amendment in 2016.

secs.t: Basel Convention - concern, transboundary waste trade, Ban Amendment

x: Exam angle: match Basel to hazardous waste, Montreal to the ozone layer and Kyoto to greenhouse gases. "Biodiversity" is the usual wrong option for Basel.
The Basel Convention controls the transboundary movement of hazardous wastes and their disposal, while promoting environmentally sound management.
India implements the Basel Convention through the Prior Informed Consent mechanism under the
Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016

secs.t: Kigali Amendment - HFC uses, gases targeted, India's group and years

x: The Kigali Amendment is legally binding and phases down
hydrofluorocarbons
, or HFCs.
HFCs replaced ODS in cooling equipment, do not deplete ozone, and possess high global warming potential.
The overall target is an
phase-down of HFC use by the late 2040s.
Developing Group 1 includes China and has a 2020–22 baseline, a 2024 freeze and an 80% final cut by 2045.
The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change directed Central and State authorities to stop granting environmental clearances for new or additional HFC production after 31 December 2027.

secs.t: World Ozone Day - date, theme

x: Observed on
16 September
, the day the Montreal Protocol was signed.
It was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in
the day marked
10 years since the Kigali Amendment was adopted

secs.t: Minamata Convention - mercury, sources, origin of name

x: The Minamata Convention protects human health and the environment from anthropogenic emissions of mercury and mercury compounds across the mercury lifecycle.
Major sources include coal-fired power plants, artisanal and small-scale gold mining, industrial processes and waste.
The Convention is named after Minamata, Japan, where factory wastewater contaminated local fish with mercury and poisoned people in the 1950s.

secs.t: Stockholm Convention - initial POPs, new chemicals, India's ratification

x: POPs are toxic chemicals that persist for long periods, build up in living tissue and travel long distances.
The other eight initial POPs were
aldrin, chlordane, dieldrin, endrin, heptachlor, hexachlorobenzene, mirex and toxaphene
The
POPs Review Committee
, or POPRC, assesses candidate chemicals for possible listing.
The seven additional POPs ratified by India in 2020 included
chlordecone, hexabromobiphenyl, pentachlorobenzene, hexabromocyclododecane and hexachlorobutadiene

secs.t: Rotterdam Convention - PIC procedure, chemicals listed

x: India’s Designated National Authorities are the Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilisers and the Ministry of Agriculture, while the Official Contact Points are located in MoEF&CC.
The Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions share one joint secretariat under the United Nations Environment Programme.
In India, coordination of these three conventions is undertaken by the
Hazardous Substances Management Division of MoEFCC

secs.t: Vienna Convention 1985 and India Cooling Action Plan

x: The Vienna Convention provides the framework, while the Montreal Protocol supplies the specific phase-out action adopted under that framework.
The six thematic areas are space cooling in buildings, cold chain, servicing sector, domestic or indigenous production, research and development, and transport.
One of the ICAP targets is to train
1 lakh
servicing technicians by 2037-38.
The Ozone Cell is India’s National Ozone Unit for the phase-out of ozone-depleting substances.

secs.t: Ozone hole - location, season, PSCs, recovery

x: The Antarctic ozone hole is a seasonal phenomenon, with maximum thinning during
Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November
In the extremely cold polar vortex, polar stratospheric clouds provide surfaces that convert stable chlorine into active forms.
The ozone hole was detected over Antarctica in the mid-1980s, and a British survey reported it in 1985.

secs.t: UV radiation effects - target-wise

x: A 1% loss of ozone is associated with an approximately 2% increase in harmful UV radiation.
Increased bone density
is not included among them.
Damage to plankton and aquatic larvae affects the base and links of marine food chains, causing food-chain disruption.
Increased UV radiation degrades materials such as wood, plastic, rubber and fabrics.

secs.t: Environmental treaties - focus identification

x: The Vienna Convention was adopted in 1985, the Basel Convention in 1989, the Kyoto Protocol in 1997 and the Cartagena Protocol in 2000.
The Basel Convention concerns the movement of hazardous waste.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Basel concerns waste, Rotterdam concerns prior consent in trade, Stockholm concerns persistent chemicals, and Minamata concerns mercury.
Both the Montreal Protocol and the Vienna Convention are associated with protection of the ozone layer.
The reported dense stratospheric ozone pocket was at
21–23 km over the North Bay of Bengal
Andhra Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister
K. Pawan Kalyan
delivered the cited World Ozone Day 2026 message.
