rows.title: International climate initiatives - UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol, CDM, Paris Agreement, key COP outcomes, IPCC assessment reports
sub: Group-II M2-B-95: International climate architecture - UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement
Group-II M2-B-96: Recent Conference of the Parties outcomes and the loss and damage fund
Group-II M2-B-97: IPCC assessment reports - key findings and their significance for India
Group-II M2-B-98: India's participation and role in climate negotiations - equity, CBDR and the developing-country position

secs.t: COP outcomes and host cities - key decisions, declarations India did not sign

x: The Copenhagen Accord, Paris rulebook and Glasgow Climate Pact are associated with COP15, COP24 and COP26 respectively.
COP26 was held at Glasgow in 2021 and was associated with the Glasgow Climate Pact, coal phase-down language and India's Panchamrit.
COP28, held at Dubai, UAE, in 2023, produced the first Global Stocktake and the call for a transition away from fossil fuels.
India did not sign the Global Methane Pledge and stayed out of the Glasgow Leaders' Declaration on Forests and Land Use
COP22 was held at Marrakech, COP23 at Bonn under Fiji's presidency, and COP25 at Madrid under Chile's presidency.

COP21 in Paris produced the Paris Agreement; COP26 in Glasgow produced the Glasgow Climate Pact; COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh produced the Loss and Damage Fund; and COP28 in Dubai produced the Global Stocktake and the “transition away” wording.

secs.t: Kyoto Protocol - adoption, entry into force, binding parties, periods, mechanisms

x: The Kyoto Protocol was adopted at Kyoto on 11 December 1997 during COP3 and was the first legally binding climate agreement.
Under CDM, an Annex I country invests in an emission-reduction project in a developing country and earns Certified Emission Reductions (CERs).

International Emissions Trading involves allowances traded among Annex I countries; CDM generates CERs from developing-country projects; Joint Implementation generates ERUs from projects in other Annex I countries.
Both statements are true, and the differentiated treatment of industrialised and developing countries explains why binding targets were limited to Annex I parties.

secs.t: Paris Agreement - temperature goal, NDCs, Article 6, global stocktake

x: The Agreement binds parties to procedural obligations such as preparing, communicating and reporting NDCs, but the emission targets themselves are nationally determined and not legally binding.
Under the ratchet mechanism, each new NDC must represent progression beyond the previous one and is informed by the Global Stocktake.
Article 6.4 establishes the UN-run Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM).
The Article 6.4 mechanism replaces the Kyoto CDM, corresponding adjustments prevent double counting, and Article 6 was made fully operational at COP29.
India’s updated emissions-intensity target is a
45 percent
reduction from the 2005 level by 2030; the earlier target was 33–35 percent.
The 2035 NDC includes a 47% intensity cut, 60% non-fossil power capacity and an additional sink of 3.5–4.0 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent.

secs.t: Climate finance and risk initiatives - Global Shield, GCF, GEF, Adaptation Fund, L&D Fund

x: Exam angle: in APPSC 2024 both Global Shield statements were keyed
wrong
("None of the above"), so check who founded it and where it was launched.
The GCF was criticised for a seven-year delay in clearing Nepal’s $49.9 million proposal relating to glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) risk.
The Adaptation Fund was established under the Kyoto Protocol, is financed by a 2% share of CDM CER proceeds, and NABARD is India’s National Implementing Entity.

secs.t: Treaty and its environmental goal

x: The
Basel Convention
concerns the transboundary movement of hazardous waste, not greenhouse-gas reduction.
The Montreal Protocol addresses ozone-depleting substances, Basel concerns hazardous-waste movement, CBD concerns biodiversity and Ramsar concerns wetlands.
The Ramsar Convention was adopted in 1971 in Iran and concerns wetlands.
CITES regulates trade in endangered species, is associated with Washington and was signed in 1973.

secs.t: Other climate initiatives - founder or type

x: Climate Action Tracker is an independent scientific analysis initiative of
Climate Analytics and the NewClimate Institute
The New York Declaration on Forests was endorsed at the 2014 UN Climate Summit and is voluntary and non-binding, with the objective of halting deforestation.
The New York Declaration on Forests provided the basis for the Bonn Challenge target of restoring
350 million hectares

secs.t: UNFCCC - adoption, Annex parties, CBDR-RC

x: The UNFCCC was adopted on 9 May 1992, opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit, entered into force on 21 March 1994, and has its secretariat in Bonn, Germany.
The objective of the UNFCCC is to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system.
The UNFCCC has 198 Parties; the COP is its supreme body and meets annually, while the SBI and SBSTA meet mid-year in Bonn.
CBDR-RC recognises differentiated historical responsibility and capabilities; developed countries that caused most historical emissions are expected to take the lead.
The Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement are the two instruments associated with the UNFCCC; their governing meetings are referred to as CMP and CMA respectively.

secs.t: IPCC - founding bodies, AR1-AR6, working groups, AR7

x: The IPCC was set up in 1988 by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
The IPCC has 195 member countries, its reports are policy-relevant but not policy-prescriptive, and it shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize with Al Gore.
The IPCC’s First Assessment Report (AR1), published in 1990, fed into the UNFCCC, which was adopted in 1992 at the Rio Earth Summit process.
The AR7 cycle began in July 2023, with Working Group reports expected around mid-2028 and the Synthesis Report by late 2029.

secs.t: CDM in India and negotiating blocs

x: CDM projects in developing countries such as India earned Certified Emission Reductions, or CERs.
India requested dedicated agenda space for Article 9.1, which obliges developed countries to provide climate finance to developing countries.

secs.t: Treaties - which address greenhouse gases

x: The
Kyoto Protocol
, adopted in 1997, addresses greenhouse-gas reductions.
The Rotterdam Convention establishes the Prior Informed Consent procedure for certain hazardous chemicals and pesticides in international trade.

secs.t: Carbon credits

x: One carbon credit represents one tonne of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions reduced, avoided or removed.
India signed the Joint Crediting Mechanism with Japan in August 2025 under
Article 6.2
The first Article 6.4 credits went to
a clean-cooking project in Myanmar

secs.t: Global Stocktake and Paris timelines

x: New NDCs are submitted every five years.
Article 13 establishes the Enhanced Transparency Framework, including common reporting through Biennial Transparency Reports.

secs.t: Withdrawal and re-entry

x: A party may give notice of withdrawal three years after the Agreement entered into force for it, and the withdrawal takes effect one year after the notice.
The United States announced withdrawal in 2017, its withdrawal became effective on 4 November 2020, and it rejoined on 19 February 2021.

secs.t: COP27 outcomes

x: Exam angle: multi-statement COP27 questions (APPSC-G1 2022: I, III, IV correct) - read each clause on dates and temperature targets.
COP27 reaffirmed the goal of keeping warming well below 2°C and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. It did not replace these targets with an exact 1°C limit.
The Sharm el-Sheikh Adaptation Agenda contained 30 outcomes intended to benefit 4 billion people by 2030.

secs.t: Climate initiatives launched at COPs - founders

x: The Global Methane Pledge was launched at COP26 by the United States and the European Union and aims to cut methane emissions by 30 per cent from 2020 levels by 2030.
The Glasgow Breakthroughs cover power, road transport, steel, hydrogen and agriculture.

secs.t: COP28 - UAE Consensus, first GST

x: The UAE Consensus was the first COP decision calling for a transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.
COP28 included pledges to triple renewable capacity to 11,000 GW and double energy-efficiency gains to 4 per cent per year by 2030.
COP28 concluded the first Global Stocktake and operationalised the Loss and Damage Fund.

secs.t: India's positions at recent COPs

x: India advocated a
phase-down
, rather than a phase-out, of unabated coal power at COP26.
India called for a dedicated agenda on developed-country finance obligations at
Bonn SB64
India criticised the US$300 billion annual NCQG target as
inadequate
The Prime Minister announced India's bid for COP33 at COP28 on 1 December 2023; it was withdrawn in April 2026 after a review of commitments for 2028.
The earlier goal was to mobilise US$100 billion annually, and it was a major focus at COP26.

secs.t: Loss and Damage Fund (FRLD)

x: The Fund was agreed at COP27 in 2022, operationalised at COP28 in 2023, opened to applications at COP30, and the World Bank’s interim role extends until COP33 in 2028.
The Fund covers economic and non-economic losses resulting from both sudden-onset and slow-onset events.
The start-up phase is under the Barbados Implementation Modalities.

secs.t: COP29 - NCQG and Article 6

x: COP29 set a core mobilisation goal of US$300 billion annually by 2035 for developed countries and made a wider call for US$1.3 trillion annually from all sources by 2035.
COP29 was held in
Baku in November 2024
, where the NCQG figures were finalised.
The UN-supervised Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism under Article 6.4 is intended to replace the
Clean Development Mechanism

secs.t: COP30 Belem - outcomes and NDC 3.0

x: The COP30 outcome was called the
Belém Political Package
and was framed in a ‘mutirão’ spirit.
COP30 agreed to
at least triple adaptation finance
The Belem 4x pledge aims to quadruple sustainable fuels by 2035.
NDC 3.0 calls for economy-wide, all-gas pledges aligned with the 1.5°C objective and due for COP30.

secs.t: Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5 C - time window, pathways, 2030 CO2 cut, net-zero timing

x: Exam angle: fill-in-the-blank on "2030-2052", "45% by 2030 from 2010 levels" and "net zero by 2050".
The stated pathway requires global emissions to peak before 2025, reach net zero by mid-century, and obtain 70–85% of electricity from renewables by 2050.
AR6 Working Group I placed the remaining carbon budget for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5°C at about
500 GtCO2
from 2020.
Working Group I corresponds to the Physical Science Basis; Working Group II to Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability; Working Group III to Mitigation; and the final report is the Synthesis Report.

secs.t: AR6 India-relevant findings - heat, sea level, monsoon, Himalayan glaciers

x: The IPCC AR6 indicates that
India is warming faster than the global average
and is experiencing more frequent and intense heatwaves.
AR6 associates erratic monsoons with severe floods, identifies risks to Mumbai and Chennai from sea-level rise, and reports that high mountains are warming at twice the global average.
Black carbon lowers the albedo of snow, causing it to absorb more solar energy and thereby accelerating melting.

secs.t: Other special reports - Land; Ocean and Cryosphere

x: The Ocean and Cryosphere report highlighted that marine heatwaves became more frequent, along with coral bleaching and fisheries impacts.
These findings are associated with the IPCC
Special Report on Ocean and Cryosphere
, released in September 2019.

secs.t: Shared Socioeconomic Pathways - meaning, scenario names

x: SSPs are narratives concerning future population, economic and policy conditions that are used with forcing levels in AR6 scenarios.
SSPs replaced the four
Representative Concentration Pathways
, or RCPs, used in AR5.
SSP3 represents Regional Rivalry.
is one of the AR6 illustrative scenarios.
RCP8.5 was introduced in 2011 as one of the four RCPs.

secs.t: AR7 cycle - timeline, Special Report on Climate Change and Cities

x: AR7 began in July 2023, but its Working Group reports are expected only from about mid-2028 and its Synthesis Report by late 2029; therefore AR6 remains the current authority in the interim.

secs.t: IPCC Nobel Peace Prize - year, co-recipient

x: The IPCC shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize equally with former United States Vice President
Al Gore

secs.t: India's mitigation constraints - coal, technology and finance, development priorities

x: India argues that developed countries should provide clean, affordable technology and finance to support the transition.
Gevra is a coal mine in Chhattisgarh and Rajmahal is a coal mine in Jharkhand; both are on the LINGO list of carbon bombs.
India links its later net-zero target to development priorities, a large population needing growth and industrialisation, and continuing coal dependence.

secs.t: Climate equity - historical emissions, per capita comparisons, carbon space

x: All four statements express the climate-equity position: historical responsibility lies mainly with developed countries, India's per capita emissions are lower, developing countries seek carbon space, and those least responsible may suffer most.
The Loss and Damage Fund associated with COP27 in 2022 was regarded as an ethical win in the context of climate justice.

secs.t: India's stand on unilateral trade measures - EU CBAM, deforestation regulation

x: CBAM entered its transitional phase in 2023, its definitive phase on 1 January 2026, aims to prevent carbon leakage, and exempts firms subject to an equivalent domestic carbon price.
India argues that CBAM violates the principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC) and amounts to green protectionism.
The 12th BRICS Environment Ministers' Meeting in New Delhi, during India's chairmanship, called CBAM
unilateral, punitive, discriminatory and protectionist

secs.t: Climate justice - G20 New Delhi and Voice of Global South summits

x: The G20 New Delhi Leaders' Declaration adopted a
Green Development Pact
The Global Biofuels Alliance was launched at the
G20 New Delhi Summit
in September 2023.
Mission LiFE is India's idea-level contribution centred on
individual behaviour change
The declaration was associated with the BRICS meeting at Rio in July 2025 and supported Global South demands.

secs.t: UNFCCC COP hosted by India - edition, declaration adopted

x: Exam angle: match the COP with its city and outcome (COP8 Delhi, COP21 Paris, COP26 Glasgow Pact, COP27 Loss and Damage Fund, COP29 NCQG, COP30 Belém).

COP21 adopted the Paris Agreement, COP26 produced the Glasgow Climate Pact, COP27 established the Loss and Damage Fund, and COP29 is associated with the New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The three stated 2035 goals were a 35% electricity share in final energy, halving the growth of global waste, and reducing building energy intensity by 25%.
Because the CMP and CMA work by consensus, every party can effectively block agreement, leading to the criticism that they resemble 'hop-on, hop-off buses'.
BRICS
has viewed the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism as sidestepping UNFCCC principles.
Climate refugees displaced by sea-level rise fall outside the legal scope of the
1951 Refugee Convention
Nepal's request after the August 2026 glacial-collapse flood was viewed as
an early test of the Fund
for Responding to Loss and Damage.
The agreed scientific baseline informs negotiations, and the 1.5°C and net-zero-by-2050 benchmarks rest on SR1.5 and AR6.
India's 2070 net-zero target is criticised as late, while India defends it using the principles of common but differentiated responsibilities and development needs.

rows.title: India's climate commitments - NDCs, Panchamrit, net-zero 2070, LiFE mission, ISA, CDRI, carbon market
sub: Group-II M2-B-99: India's climate commitments - NDCs, Panchamrit and net zero by 2070
Group-II M2-B-101: India's climate initiatives - International Solar Alliance, CDRI, LiFE and the carbon credit trading scheme

secs.t: India's NDC - INDC 2015 vs updated NDC 2022 (and NDC 3.0 for 2035)

x: Exam angle: the target is non-fossil
installed capacity
, not generation. UPSC notes say "40% of power generation", which is wrong.
The 2015 INDC target was to reduce emissions intensity of GDP by
below 2005 levels by 2030.
India communicated its updated NDC in
August 2022
, formalising the Panchamrit commitments in the NDC framework.
India crossed the 50% non-fossil share in installed electric capacity in
June 2025
, five years ahead of the 2030 target timeline.
The 2015 INDC target was 33–35%, the 2022 target was 45%, and NDC 3.0 sets 47% emissions-intensity reduction and 60% non-fossil installed capacity.
The correct sequence is INDC submission in October 2015, updated NDC communication in August 2022, crossing 50% capacity in June 2025 and NDC 3.0 approval in March 2026.

secs.t: ISA and CDRI - HQ, launch, first summit, treaty status, new members

x: Although the ISA initially began with the idea of bringing together sunshine countries between the tropics, its membership is now open to all UN member states.
The United States joined in 2021, announced withdrawal in January 2026, and had contributed about $2.1 million, or roughly 1 per cent of ISA funds.
IRIS, or Infrastructure for Resilient Island States, focuses on Small Island Developing States and was launched at COP26 in 2021.

secs.t: Mission LiFE - full form, launch, P3, LiFE actions

x: The LiFE idea was introduced at COP26, while Mission LiFE was launched at Kevadia in October 2022 in the presence of the UN Secretary-General.
P3 stands for ‘
Pro-Planet People
’, the community that Mission LiFE seeks to build through environmentally responsible behaviour.
The LiFE themes include saving energy and water, rejecting single-use plastic, sustainable food systems, reducing waste and e-waste, and healthy lifestyles.

secs.t: Net-zero target and Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy

x: India invokes the principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR) and its development requirements to justify the 2070 target, later than the 2050 targets of most developed countries.

The seven transitions include low-carbon electricity systems, low-carbon transport, urban adaptation and efficient buildings, decoupling growth from industrial emissions, CO2 removal, forest and vegetation cover, and low-carbon finance.

The Panchamrit commitments were announced on 1 November 2021; the net-zero target was announced at COP26 in 2021; the LT-LEDS was submitted in November 2022; and the Net Zero Portal was launched in September 2026.

secs.t: Climate Change Performance Index - publisher, India's rank

x: The CCPI is published by Germanwatch, the NewClimate Institute and Climate Action Network (CAN) International.
The CCPI is released at the Conference of the Parties (COP) on climate change.
India was ranked
9th
in the 2019 CCPI referred to in the APPSC 2018 question.

secs.t: Panchamrit - the five COP26 commitments

x: Exam angle: memory hook 500-50-1-45-2070. The trap is capacity versus generation.
Approximately 51 percent had been achieved by September 2025 for the commitment concerning the share of energy requirements from renewables, expressed in the NDC as installed capacity.

The renewable-energy pledge is expressed as 50 percent of energy requirements, or 50 percent of installed capacity in the NDC formulation, while the separate non-fossil pledge is 500 GW; both are targeted for 2030.

secs.t: Green Credit Programme and carbon market

x: The Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE), Dehradun, administers the Green Credit Programme.
The programme covers activities such as tree planting, water management, sustainable agriculture, waste management, air-pollution reduction, mangroves, ecomark and sustainable buildings.
Entities that beat their notified GHG Emission Intensity targets earn tradeable Carbon Credit Certificates.
Compliance entities receive intensity targets, underperforming entities buy certificates, and the offset mechanism covers voluntary projects in ten sectors.
Green credits may be earned for voluntary actions such as
mangrove conservation
, tree plantation, water management, sustainable agriculture, waste management and air-pollution reduction.

secs.t: India-led climate coalitions - GBA, LeadIT, Mission Innovation, Big Cat Alliance

x: The Global Biofuels Alliance was launched during India’s G20 Presidency; LeadIT was set up by India and Sweden in 2019; Mission Innovation began at COP21 in 2015; and the Big Cat Alliance was launched at Mysuru in April 2023.

The International Solar Alliance was launched at COP21; CDRI at the 2019 UN Climate Action Summit; the Global Biofuels Alliance during India's 2023 G20 Presidency; and ACITI on the sidelines of G20 Johannesburg in November 2025.

secs.t: India's negotiating stance - climate justice, per-capita emissions, finance, NDC 2035

x: All three statements describe India’s stated negotiating position: equity, climate justice, CBDR-RC, and continuity with incremental advance within its equitable share.
The first Biennial Transparency Report indicated that
over 20 percent
of emissions in 2022 came from industry.
The reported breakdown was 13 percent from fuel use in manufacturing and construction and 9 percent from industrial processes, together exceeding 20 percent.

secs.t: Carbon sink target - forest and tree cover, Green India Mission, trees outside forests

x: The official estimate for carbon sink addition during 2005–2019 was
1.97 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent
The original 2020 sequestration goal of 50–60 million tonnes per year is now folded into the 2030 carbon-sink target.
Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam was a supporting drive launched in 2024.
MISHTI was associated with mangrove coverage of more than
540 square kilometres

secs.t: Energy transition targets - non-fossil capacity, Green Hydrogen Mission, storage

x: 291.52 GW total non-fossil, 282.74 GW renewable energy including large hydro, and 8.78 GW nuclear capacity.
The Economic Survey 2025–26 places India
fourth
in installed renewable energy capacity; another cited source gives a third-place ranking.
The first utility-scale standalone BESS is a
180 MW
project developed by IndiGrid in Gujarat.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The audit found weak convergence with CAMPA and MGNREGS and inadequate funding; it did not find excessive funding and complete convergence.
The demand seeks to allow smaller firms to monetise avoided emissions through wider access to the carbon market.
The CAG found gaps in the Green India Mission, particularly
poor convergence with CAMPA and MGNREGS
The Net Zero Portal and NAPCC Dashboard were launched by
the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

rows.title: National Action Plan on Climate Change - the eight national missions; State Action Plans on Climate Change
sub: Group-II M2-B-100: National Action Plan on Climate Change - the eight missions; State Action Plans and AP's plan

secs.t: National missions - count, names and nodal ministry

x: Exam angle: "Which is NOT a NAPCC mission?" - distractors are usually schemes such as Swachh Bharat, Ujjwala or AMRUT.
The
Perform, Achieve and Trade
(PAT) scheme is included in the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency and is associated with the Ministry of Power and BEE.
The National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem assesses Himalayan vulnerability through 12 thematic areas.
The
National Mission on Clean Air
is not one of the original eight NAPCC missions.

secs.t: NAPCC - release, Council and scope

x: Four
of the eight core missions focus on adaptation, while the NAPCC as a whole addresses both adaptation and mitigation.
The Economic Survey 2025–26 uses a nine-mission description by adding health, while the officially tested count of core missions remains eight.
The National Action Plan on Climate Change was launched in 2008, the Climate Change Knowledge Portal was launched in 2020, and the Net Zero target year is 2070.

secs.t: AP climate action - Climate Change Cell, AP SAPCC, FFF-AP

x: The exclusive cell created by Andhra Pradesh in November 2022 is now called the
Andhra Pradesh State Climate Change Cell (APSCCC)
The revised AP SAPCC covers 2025–30, includes eight energy-sector adaptation measures and is based on vulnerability to rising temperatures, variable rainfall and extreme events.
Heatwaves, droughts, floods and cyclones affect water, agriculture, food security and health.

secs.t: Mission objectives - GIM, NWM, PAT, NMSA

x: The three sub-missions concern forest quality, forest and tree cover with ecosystem restoration, and incomes of forest-dependent people.
The National Water Mission includes a public water database, impact assessment, citizen and State action, focus on over-exploited areas and improved water-use efficiency through basin-level IWRM.
PAT rewards industries that beat their energy-saving targets with tradable Energy Saving Certificates.
NMSA includes Rainfed Area Development, On-Farm Water Management and Soil Health Management, along with a Sub-Mission on Agroforestry.

secs.t: SAPCC - states, vulnerability, state cells

x: States have moved from broad mitigation-centric plans in 2010–15 towards district-specific, risk-based adaptation plans from 2020 onwards, linked with social schemes and local institutions.
NMSKCC supports State Climate Change Centres and vulnerability assessments at both State and district levels.
The proposal is to introduce climate budgeting through State Finance Departments by means of
a budget circular

secs.t: New missions proposed - health, coastal, wind, waste-to-energy

x: All four—Wind Energy, Health, Coastal Areas and Waste-to-Energy—were proposed as new missions around 2015.
Of the proposed new missions, only the
Health Mission
has been counted in the Economic Survey 2025–26 as the ninth mission.
Nuclear and Green Hydrogen are newer initiatives that advance the net-zero-by-2070 objective but remain outside the original eight missions.

secs.t: Climate Change Action Programme and NAFCC

x: CCAP is a 2014 scheme of the
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
(MoEFCC).
CCAP builds capacity, supports SAPCCs and strengthens the scientific and analytical base.
NAFCC was established in 2015 as a central sector scheme to finance adaptation projects of States and Union Territories in vulnerable sectors.
NABARD
is the National Implementing Entity for NAFCC-funded adaptation projects.

secs.t: Governance - Executive Committee, MoEFCC climate division

x: The Prime Minister’s Council on Climate Change sets policy, while the Executive Committee on Climate Change, under the Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister, coordinates it.
The MoEFCC Climate Change Division is the nodal unit for UNFCCC negotiations and coordination of the National Action Plan on Climate Change.
India’s National Statement at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, was delivered on
17 November 2025

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Adaptation spending rose from 3.7 per cent of GDP in FY16 to
5.6 per cent
in FY22.
The NAPCC is the domestic vehicle for implementing India’s
Nationally Determined Contributions
(NDCs).
Tamil Nadu has a Governing Council on Climate Change headed by the Chief Minister and also has a TN Green Climate Company.

rows.title: Environmental pollution - types, sources and impacts (overview)
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-85

secs.t: Major pollution disasters - year, place, pollutant

x: Exam angle: Bhopal = gas leakage / MIC / 1984 is asked almost every year.
The Los Angeles smog was photochemical smog, produced when sunlight acted on nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons from vehicle exhaust, particularly at about 24–32°C.
The correct sequence is Los Angeles smog (1943), Minamata disease (1956), Bhopal gas tragedy (1984), and Chernobyl (1986).

secs.t: Pollution type - major primary source - impacts

x: The major primary sources of air pollution are industrial emissions, including sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulate matter, together with vehicle exhaust.
Chemical fertilisers, pesticides and industrial waste are major sources of soil pollution, which can reduce soil fertility, contaminate crops and disturb soil fauna.
Marble cancer is associated with acid rain, particularly sulphur dioxide.

secs.t: Environmental research and monitoring bodies - headquarters

x: The CPCB was established in 1974 under the Water Act and was renamed in 1988.
The Wildlife Institute of India is headquartered in Dehradun; CSE in New Delhi; and both the Botanical Survey of India and Zoological Survey of India in Kolkata.

secs.t: Toxic pollutants and their sources

x: Coal ash can contain heavy metals such as
arsenic, mercury, lead, cadmium and chromium
; its disposal can therefore pollute soil.
Agricultural fertilisers and livestock excreta contribute approximately 77–80% of ammonia emissions in the NCR, according to the cited synthesis report.
Such burning can release dioxins, furans, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, lead, cadmium and mercury.

secs.t: Pollutant classification

x: Plastics and DDT are examples of non-biodegradable pollutants.
A chimney is a point source, vehicles along a highway represent a line source, and farm runoff is a diffuse or non-point source.
Xenobiotics are synthetic chemicals foreign to living systems, such as pesticides, PCBs and plastics, and they generally resist degradation.

secs.t: Comprehensive Environmental Pollution Index (CEPI)

x: CEPI was developed in 2009 by the CPCB in association with
IIT Delhi
CEPI scores industrial clusters on a scale from
CEPI considers pollutant, pathway and receptor, with the receptor representing exposed people, and covers air, water and land pollution.
A CEPI score of 70 or above indicates a critically polluted cluster.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: PARIVESH 3.0 is described as a single-window mechanism for environmental governance and approvals.
The Andhra Pradesh Common Zoning Regulations 2026 recognise
nine
land-use categories, including provisions noting white and green industries.
APPCB chairman P. Krishnaiah urged an eco-friendly Bhogi.
The Environment Audit Rules, 2025 provide for third-party auditors to assess compliance.

rows.title: Air pollution - sources, pollutants, NAAQS, AQI, National Clean Air Programme, stubble burning
sub: Group-II M2-B-74: Air pollution - pollutants, sources, standards (NAAQS), AQI and health impacts
Group-II M2-B-75: Air pollution control - National Clean Air Programme, stubble burning and vehicular emission measures
Group-II M2-B-91: Acid rain - causes, chemistry, effects and control measures

secs.t: Pollution sources - natural vs anthropogenic, primary vs secondary, SO2

x: Vehicles emit pollutants such as carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, VOCs, particulate matter and unburnt hydrocarbons.
Classical or London smog consists of sulphur dioxide, smoke and particulates mixed with fog under cold and humid conditions.
Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight, producing pollutants such as ozone and PAN.
Ammonium sulphate forms through the atmospheric interaction of
sulphur dioxide and ammonia
and contributes substantially to particulate pollution.
The Asian Brown Cloud is a dry-season layer of soot, black carbon and aerosols over South Asia and the Indian Ocean, arising mainly from biomass and fossil-fuel burning.

secs.t: Pollutants → health effect; acid rain

x: Exam angle: "pollutant from vehicles that reduces O2 carrying capacity of blood" = carbon monoxide.

Carbon monoxide reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity; sulphur dioxide irritates the eyes and respiratory system; lead damages the brain; and ground-level ozone causes asthma and eye irritation.
Carbon monoxide
combines functionally with blood haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood, causing giddiness and potentially death.
Magnetite particles from combustion and vehicle brake wear have been found in human brain tissue and have a possible link with Alzheimer's disease.

secs.t: NCAP - launch, target, cities, PRANA, rankings

x: Exam angle: NCAP is the answer for "government initiative to control industrial emissions".
The original NCAP target was a
20–30 per cent
reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 by 2024, using 2017 as the base year.
PRANA means
Portal for Regulation of Air-pollution in Non-Attainment cities
and is used to track NCAP progress.
The reported figure is 38 LMT, meaning 38 lakh metric tonnes, whereas the option states the figure in an altered form as 38 lakh metric tonnes but omits the official LMT presentation.
103 cities reduced PM10, 22 cities met the relevant NAAQS, and PRANA tracks NCAP progress.
The NGT observed that 86 per cent of spending had gone to road dust and directed that funding be tied to measured PM reductions, while asking southern States to execute their plans.

secs.t: WHO Air Quality Guidelines 2021 and IQAir

x: NCR winter PM2.5 averages have been reported at nearly
35 times
the WHO limit.
Fossil-fuel air pollution caused about
1.72 million
premature deaths in India in 2022.
India’s NAAQS cover 12 pollutants, including PM10, PM2.5, SO2, NO2, CO, O3, NH3, lead, benzene, benzo(a)pyrene, arsenic and nickel.
Visakhapatnam emerged as Andhra Pradesh’s pollution hotspot; its PM2.5 increased by 33 per cent from January 2024 to April 2026 and exceeded national limits.

secs.t: AQI and NAAQS - categories, pollutants, NAMP, SAFAR

x: The NAQI covers eight pollutants—PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3 and Pb—on a 0–500 scale.
Benzene
is included in the 12-pollutant NAAQS set, but not among the eight pollutants used in the NAQI list stated here.
The correct matches are 51–100—Satisfactory, 201–300—Poor, 301–400—Very poor and 401–500—Severe.
The
Severe
category, covering AQI values 401–500, is represented by maroon.
The NAAQS cover 12 pollutants, including the eight AQI pollutants plus benzene, benzo(a)pyrene, arsenic and nickel.
NAMP regularly monitors
SO2, NO2, PM10 and PM2.5
The MoES system provides forecasts at 400 m resolution and is tied to the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP).

secs.t: AP air quality action

x: APPCB operates 12 CAAQM stations and 19 LED display boards; nine additional stations were being installed.
The action plan covers 123 urban local bodies, including 17 municipal corporations.
The burning of tyres, plastic and flex can release dioxins, furans, sulphur dioxide and heavy metals.
The school Eco-Clubs operate under the AP National Green Corps and have existed since 2002–03.
Vijayawada Ward 60 ranked second nationally, Ward 31 was best in the State, and VMC received ₹30 lakh.

secs.t: Control technologies - catalytic converters, cloud seeding, indoor pollution

x: Catalytic converters use
platinum, palladium and rhodium
as catalyst metals.
Cloud seeding may use silver iodide, potassium iodide, dry ice and common salt.
Scrubbers, electrostatic precipitators and FGD are pollution-control technologies; pelletisation is an ex-situ method of managing crop residue.
Indoor air pollution can arise from
smoke from solid fuels
, dust, mould, pollen, radon and carbon monoxide.

secs.t: Bioindicators - lichens

x: Lichens indicate
sulphur dioxide
pollution and disappear from areas with high SO2 levels.
Lichens are sensitive to SO2, while mosses accumulate and indicate heavy-metal deposition.

secs.t: Stubble burning and NCR measures - CAQM, decomposer, machinery, GRAP

x: Paddy and wheat stubble is mainly burnt during
October–November in Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh
GRAP Stage I corresponds to Poor, Stage II to Very poor, Stage III to Severe (401–450), and Stage IV to Severe+ above 450.
Bihar suspended the DBT registration of 1,807 farmers for stubble burning during 2025–26.

secs.t: Indoor air pollution

x: Dust, mould, pollen, radon and mosquito-coil smoke are all sources of indoor air pollution.
Indoor air pollution is linked to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and heart disease.
Indoor pollution also comes from dust, smoke, pesticides, gases and mosquito coils.
The IntrCity study reported that air inside intercity bus cabins was two to three times the WHO limits.

secs.t: Methods to control air pollution - transport and cleaner fuels

x: Cycling, walking, public transport, green belts, Miyawaki micro-forests and dust-free roads help control air pollution.

The Methanol Economy concerns methanol fuel or blending; SATAT concerns compressed biogas; the National Green Hydrogen Mission concerns hydrogen; and the Ethanol Blending Programme requires support for E20 in new vehicles.
The material states that all new vehicles must support E20 and that about 95% of pre-2020 vehicles are not fully compatible.

secs.t: Vehicular emission control

x: A catalytic converter converts carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides into carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen.

BS-III began in the specified areas on 1 April 2005; BS-VI became nationwide on 1 April 2020; the vehicle scrappage policy was introduced in 2021; and Stage II added Real Driving Emission tests thereafter.

secs.t: Industrial emission control devices

x: An electrostatic precipitator removes fine particulates, particularly fly ash, from industrial emissions.
Bag filters use fabric filtration; cyclone separators use centrifugal force for coarse particles; wet scrubbers remove gases and particles; and FGD can remove up to 95% of SO2 from flue gas.

secs.t: Emergency measures - GRAP, smog towers, cloud seeding

x: Stage I corresponds to poor AQI (201–300), Stage II to very poor (301–400), Stage III to severe (401–450), and Stage IV to severe-plus, above 450.
VAYU, or Wind Augmentation PurifYing Unit, is a roadside purifier developed by CSIR-NEERI.
Sulphur dioxide
is an air pollutant and acid-rain gas, not a cloud-seeding chemical.

secs.t: Acid rain - causative gases, sources, pH threshold

x: Exam angle: "which gases cause acid rain" and "excess of which causes acid rain" (RPSC: NOx + SO2 only).
Normal rain has a pH of about 5.6 because atmospheric carbon dioxide dissolves in water and forms weak carbonic acid.
Robert Angus Smith
coined the term “acid rain” in 1872 while describing pollution associated with coal burning in Manchester.

secs.t: Monument damage - Taj Mahal and Taj Trapezium Zone

x: The yellowing and loss of lustre of marble caused by pollution is popularly called “
marble cancer
.” Acid rain accelerates the decay of limestone and marble structures.
The Taj Trapezium Zone covers Agra, Firozabad, Mathura, Hathras and Etah in Uttar Pradesh, and Bharatpur in Rajasthan.
In 1996, the Supreme Court barred coal and coke use by TTZ industries and directed a shift to natural gas or relocation; .

secs.t: Chemistry - acids formed, relative share, wet vs dry deposition

x: Atmospheric SO2 and NOx undergo oxidation and reaction with water to form sulphuric acid (H2SO4) and nitric acid (HNO3).
Sulphuric acid accounts for approximately two-thirds of acid-rain acidity, while nitric acid accounts for about one-third.
Wet deposition occurs through rain, snow and fog, whereas dry deposition involves gases and particles attaching to dust or smoke and settling on surfaces.

secs.t: Regions most affected - global and transboundary

x: Wind can carry acid-forming pollutants hundreds of kilometres from their sources, allowing emissions from one country to affect another.
The lakes of Scandinavia, including those in Sweden and Norway, have historically received pollutants transported from the United Kingdom and central Europe.
India was identified as the largest global SO2 emitter in 2022, accounting for more than 20% of anthropogenic emissions.

secs.t: Effects - target-wise

x: Acidification lowers the pH of lake water, making conditions unsuitable for fish, frogs and insects.
Acid deposition leaches calcium and magnesium from soil and releases toxic aluminium, damaging roots.
Acid deposition corrodes limestone and marble, metals and paint, thereby damaging buildings and monuments.
Lichens are sensitive to sulphur dioxide and therefore serve as indicators of
SO2 pollution

secs.t: Control measures

x: Flue gas desulphurisation systems, commonly called scrubbers, trap SO2 in smokestacks.
Liming is a remedial measure that neutralises existing acidity; it does not prevent emissions at their source.
Low-sulphur or cleaner fuels reduce emissions, and the International Maritime Organization imposes sulphur limits on ship fuel.
The Clean Air Act reduced SO2 emissions by more than 90% in several regions of the United States.

secs.t: Acid rain monitoring in India

x: The
India Meteorological Department
monitors precipitation chemistry under the WMO Global Atmosphere Watch and BAPMoN.
The specified SO2 limits are 80 µg/m³ for 24 hours, 50 µg/m³ annually in urban areas and 20 µg/m³ annually in ecologically sensitive areas.

secs.t: International agreements - LRTAP and protocols

x: The
Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution
(LRTAP), adopted under UNECE at Geneva in 1979, was the first binding treaty on transboundary air pollution.
The Helsinki Protocol sought a 30% sulphur-emission cut; the Sofia Protocol froze NOx emissions; Gothenburg imposed pollutant caps; and LRTAP was the first binding treaty.
The Gothenburg Protocol establishes caps on SO2, NOx, ammonia and volatile organic compounds to address acidification, eutrophication and ground-level ozone.

secs.t: AP thermal power clusters - SO2 norms compliance

x: Dr NTTPS is located in the Vijayawada-Ibrahimpatnam region.
Although FGD was mandated in 2015, only 39 of 537 coal plants had installed it, and the government later relaxed the mandate citing high costs.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: In January 2026, the Supreme Court, under Chief Justice Surya Kant, told CAQM that
the causes of air pollution were still unclear
The critique states that NCAP covers only about 4% of chronically polluted towns and that PM10, rather than PM2.5, may be an inappropriate yardstick.
Clean Air for Blue Skies Day, observed on
7 September
, is marked in India as Swachh Vayu Diwas.
The WHO annual PM2.5 guideline is 5 µg/m³, compared with India's NAAQS value of 40 µg/m³; thus, the WHO limit is eight times stricter.

rows.title: Bharat Stage emission norms - evolution from BS-I to BS-VI and their implications
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I F-86

secs.t: Bharat Stage norms - nationwide implementation year

x: BS-III began in the NCR and ten major cities in 2005, became nationwide in 2010, and BS-IV became nationwide in April 2017.
The norms are notified under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 by the
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
, on the advice of CPCB and MoEFCC.
The first tractor norms were notified in 1999; Trem Stage II began on 1 June 2003 and Trem Stage III on 1 October 2005.

secs.t: Euro norms equivalence and first adoption under the Bharat Stage name

x: Exam angle: "since when Euro norms under the BS name" = 2000; BS-I also called "India 2000".
BS-I, BS-II, BS-III and BS-IV correspond respectively to Euro I, Euro II, Euro III and Euro IV.
India generally lagged Europe by approximately five years in adopting equivalent emission standards.
Euro I began in Europe in 1992.

secs.t: Transition BS-IV to BS-VI - stage skipped and why, SC deadline

x: The leapfrog was intended to address urgent urban air pollution, particularly in the Delhi-NCR region, and to close the technology gap with Europe without two successive changeovers.
The Supreme Court ordered that no BS-IV vehicle could be sold or registered from 1 April 2020.
Registering authorities cannot register non-compliant vehicles after a norm takes effect.

secs.t: Vehicular pollutants - health effects

x: NOx causes respiratory illness, particularly affecting children, and contributes to ground-level ozone formation and acid rain.
PM2.5 can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, contributing to heart and lung disease.
Lead damages the nervous system, is particularly harmful to children’s brain development, and leaded petrol was phased out in India by 2000.

secs.t: Pollutants regulated - CO, NOx, HC, PM limits; fuel sulphur per stage

x: The limits descend as BS-II—500 ppm, BS-III—350 ppm, BS-IV—50 ppm and BS-VI—10 ppm.
The BS-I limits were CO 2.72–6.90 g/km, HC+NOx 0.97–1.70 g/km and diesel PM 0.14–0.25 g/km.
The BS-VI NOx limits are 60 mg/km for petrol and 80 mg/km for diesel vehicles; the diesel PM limit is 4.5 mg/km and fuel sulphur is 10 ppm.

secs.t: BS-VI technologies - DPF, SCR, OBD, RDE

x: SCR uses a urea solution such as AdBlue to convert diesel NOx into nitrogen and water.
A DPF traps soot and periodically oxidises the accumulated particulate matter.
OBD-II continuously monitors emission performance and alerts the driver when a problem is detected.
RDE testing measures emissions on-road under real driving conditions and became applicable under BS-VI Phase 2 from April 2023.

secs.t: Implications - refinery upgrades, vehicle cost, CAFE norms

x: Refineries had to upgrade their facilities to produce BS-VI fuel with a sulphur limit of 10 ppm nationwide.
The introduction of advanced emission-control technologies increased vehicle prices, while improved public health produced offsetting social savings.
The CAFE III draft relaxed the targets by approximately
compared with the September 2025 proposal.

secs.t: Allied measures - vehicle scrappage, PUC

x: The policy provides for fitness-based de-registration through
Automated Testing Stations and Registered Vehicle Scrapping Facilities
A PUC certificate is mandatory under
the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989
Training is provided at the Automotive Research Association of India, Pune, and the Indian Institute of Petroleum, Dehradun.
CAQM, GRAP, NCAP and FAME for electric vehicles are associated measures for the NCR pollution-control context.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: BS-VII, planned for 2026–27, is expected to be equivalent to Euro 7.
Fuel sulphur declined from 500 ppm under BS-II to 10 ppm under BS-VI, a major reduction over approximately fifteen years.
The first Euro-based norm under the Bharat Stage name was BS-I, introduced in 2000, and BS-V was the only stage skipped.

rows.title: Water pollution - sources, eutrophication, Namami Gange, sewage treatment, groundwater contamination (arsenic, fluoride)
sub: Group-II M2-B-76: Water pollution - sources, eutrophication, effluent standards and groundwater contamination
Group-II M2-B-77: Water pollution control - Namami Gange, river action plans and sewage treatment

secs.t: Pollution diseases → pollutant

x: Methyl mercury biomagnified in fish and caused neurological damage in Minamata disease.
The WHO limit is 1.5 mg/L, while the BIS acceptable limit is 1.0 mg/L; the permissible BIS limit is 1.5 mg/L. National Fluorosis Day is observed on 9 September.
Excess nitrate in drinking water can cause
methaemoglobinaemia
, commonly called blue baby syndrome, in infants.

secs.t: Namami Gange and Ganga bodies

x: The sequence is 1985 Central Ganga Authority and GAP-I, 2009 NGRBA, 2011 NMCG, and 2016 National Ganga Council.
Namami Gange-II was approved in 2022 with ₹22,500 crore for
, up to 31 March 2026.

Sewerage, river-surface cleaning, afforestation, biodiversity, riverfront development, industrial effluent monitoring, Ganga Gram and public awareness are associated with the mission; uranium mining is not.
NMCG was registered as a society in 2011 and functioned as the implementing arm of the National Ganga River Basin Authority.

secs.t: Water quality parameters

x: Biochemical oxygen demand, or
BOD
, measures the oxygen needed by bacteria to decompose organic matter.
Suspended solids such as silt and clay are retained on a filter, while dissolved solids such as sodium salts pass through it.
NTU is used for turbidity, TDS represents dissolved salts, and coliform count indicates faecal contamination.
The cited Ganga bathing standard for faecal coliform is

secs.t: Eutrophication

x: The progression is oligotrophic, mesotrophic, eutrophic and, where enrichment becomes extreme, hypereutrophic.
Nitrogen and phosphorus enrichment promotes algal blooms; decomposition of the algae consumes dissolved oxygen, causing hypoxia and fish kills.
Fertiliser runoff, sewage, detergents, aquaculture effluent and airborne nitrogen can trigger eutrophication.
Dairy effluent associated with ritual offerings can have BOD far above sewage, causing rapid depletion of dissolved oxygen.

secs.t: River conservation programmes - NRCP, GRCA

x: NRCP was launched in 1995 to improve the water quality of
rivers other than the Ganga and its tributaries
through a Centre-State cost-sharing Centrally Sponsored Scheme.
NRCP funds
interception and diversion of sewage, sewage treatment plants and low-cost sanitation
measures to reduce pollution loads in rivers.
GAP-I began in 1985 for 25 main-stem Ganga towns; GAP-II began in 1993 for 60 towns on specified tributaries and rivers; NRCP began in 1995 for rivers other than the Ganga.
GRCA is a global alliance covering river cities worldwide and involves partner countries, international funding agencies and knowledge partners.

secs.t: Water quality reports and polluted river stretches

x: The cited series records 351 polluted stretches in 2018, 311 in 2022 and 296 in the latest report.
India was ranked
120th among 122 countries
in the water quality index cited in the NITI Aayog CWMI 2018.
The CPCB identified 296 polluted stretches on 271 rivers, compared with 351 stretches in 2018, and Maharashtra had the highest number.

secs.t: AP water bodies under pollution stress

x: Kolleru’s severe eutrophication is linked to conversion of the lake bed into aquaculture ponds and the inflow of farm runoff.
The municipal corporation discharges
29.6 MLD
of sewage through the Nalla Channel and draws 65 MLD of drinking water just downstream.
The reported stretch was unfit for drinking or bathing, had nitrate at 119.6 mg/L, and the city drew 65 MLD downstream of the discharge.

secs.t: Sewage treatment - technologies, gap, HAM, AMRUT

x: Activated sludge, membrane bioreactors and activated-carbon polishing are all recognised sewage-treatment technologies in the cited context.
The HAM projects under Namami Gange are intended to treat
of sewage.
The reported gap consists of piped sewerage access for only 33% of urban households, plant utilisation at 64% capacity and treatment of about 28% of urban sewage.
Raising the limit from 10 mg/L to 30 mg/L permits a higher BOD concentration in discharged effluent, which attracted criticism.

secs.t: Groundwater contamination - arsenic, fluoride, uranium, nitrate

x: The reported arsenic belt is in the Ganga-Brahmaputra plains, uranium above 30 ppb has been found in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana among other states, and 56% of districts exceed the nitrate level of 45 mg/L.
Nitrate contamination is mainly attributed to
fertiliser use
, and 56% of districts reportedly exceed 45 mg/L.
The Nalgonda technique uses
alum, lime and bleaching powder
to remove excess fluoride from water.

secs.t: Drinking water standards

x: Under BIS IS 10500, fluoride has an acceptable limit of 1.0 mg/L and a permissible limit of 1.5 mg/L.
The BIS iron limit is 0.3 mg/L, whereas no WHO value is specified in the given standards table.
The CPCB Class A standard specifies total coliform not exceeding
50 MPN/100 ml

secs.t: Effluent treatment - CETP, activated carbon, ZLD

x: A CETP is a shared treatment facility established for
clusters of small-scale industries
Andhra Pradesh runs nine CETPs, has banned discharge of non-biodegradable effluent, and has directed industries towards Zero Liquid Discharge.
Activated carbon works mainly through adsorption and can remove organic pollutants, colour, odour and pesticides.
The Tiruppur textile cluster in Tamil Nadu is an example associated with
Zero Liquid Discharge

secs.t: Point and non-point sources

x: Industrial effluent pipes and sewage outfalls are point sources because they discharge from identifiable outlets.
Sewage outfalls are identifiable point sources, while agricultural and urban runoff are diffuse sources; only about 28–30% of urban sewage is treated.
Sand mining raises turbidity and degrades river beds, thereby damaging riverine conditions.

secs.t: Ganga river governance - chronology

x: The legal base is the
River Ganga (Rejuvenation, Protection and Management) Authorities Order, 2016
, notified on 7 October 2016.
The Empowered Task Force is headed by or associated with the
Jal Shakti Minister
, while the National Ganga Council is chaired by the Prime Minister and district committees involve District Magistrates.

secs.t: CPCB designated best-use water quality classes

x: Class A is meant for drinking water after disinfection without conventional treatment, with total coliform not exceeding 50 MPN/100 ml.
Class A has a BOD limit of
not more than 2 mg/L
. Classes B and C have a limit of 3 mg/L, while Class D uses a free-ammonia criterion.
Class D specifies free ammonia up to 1.2 mg/L, while Class E uses electrical conductivity, SAR and boron limits; no dissolved-oxygen value is specified for Class E.

secs.t: Other conservation plans

x: The Yamuna Action Plan began in 1993 and focused mainly on sewage and industrial pollution control in the Delhi stretch.
The National Lake Conservation Plan began in 2001 and was merged with the wetlands programme to form NPCA in 2013.
The Yamuna Action Plan concerns sewage and industrial pollution control in the Delhi stretch of the Yamuna, not uranium remediation in Malwa.

secs.t: Ganga-specific measures

x: Arth Ganga promotes a river-linked economy through natural farming, river tourism such as dolphin safaris, treated-water reuse and support for artisans.
JALAJ livelihood centres are associated with
NMCG and the Wildlife Institute of India
under the Arth Ganga approach.
High faecal coliform is identified as the main Ganga problem, and there is a capacity mismatch between overloaded Haridwar STPs and under-used Devprayag facilities.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The identified major water-polluting sources in Andhra Pradesh are
Pharma City at Visakhapatnam, tanneries, paper mills and aquaculture
All three are identified criticisms: capacity mismatch, top-down execution and inadequate attention to river-basin planning.

Both statements are true, but the adoption of the Namami Gange model is a related policy development and is not stated as the reason for the timing of the Godavari clean-up before the 2027 Pushkarams.

rows.title: Soil, noise, thermal, marine and radioactive pollution - sources, effects and control
sub: Group-II M2-B-78: Soil, noise, thermal, marine and radioactive pollution - sources, effects and control

secs.t: Noise pollution - unit, Noise Rules 2000 zone limits, silence zones, tolerance, control devices

x: Exam angle: unit (decibel), the residential night limit, and which effects are linked to noise.
A 10 dB rise roughly doubles loudness, exposure above 85 dB may cause permanent hearing loss, and around 80 dB is regarded as hazardous noise.
The prescribed daytime limits are 75 dB(A) for industrial areas, 65 for commercial areas, 55 for residential areas and 50 for silence zones.
CPCB restricts firecrackers exceeding
125 dB
when measured at a distance of four metres from the point of bursting.
The CPCB Real Time National Ambient Noise Monitoring Network has 70 stations in seven metros: Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Lucknow and Hyderabad.
Both statements are true, and the stress response involving increased cortisol helps explain the effects of prolonged noise exposure on blood pressure and sleep.
Prolonged noise exposure may constrict blood vessels, cause digestive spasms and impair night vision.

secs.t: Pollution type → major source

x: Article 21 concerns life and personal liberty; Article 48A concerns environmental protection; Article 51A(g) is the environmental fundamental duty; SDG 6 concerns clean water and sanitation.
Marine pollution has several major sources, including land runoff, plastics, oil and sewage; it is not exclusively caused by radioactive hospital waste.
Chemical fertilisers and pesticides are identified as the major primary sources of
soil pollution

secs.t: Radioactive pollution - sources, orphan-source detection (MRDS), NDMA

x: Radon accumulation in closed rooms is a major health concern because it is
a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking
Cosmic rays originate from space, radon is a radioactive noble gas from the Earth's crust, and NORM includes uranium, thorium, radium and potassium-40 in rocks and water.
Under the NDMA plan, States and Union Territories receive MRDS for use in
metros and State capitals
to detect unclaimed radioactive material.

Natural sources include cosmic rays and radon-222; building materials may contain thorium and radon from granite; medical sources include X-rays and isotopes; nuclear sources include reactor waste and accidents.

secs.t: Marine pollution - oil spills, MARPOL, GloLitter, SACEP, microplastics, ghost nets, dead zones, Blue Flag

x: Samudra Pratap is
India’s first indigenously built Pollution Control Vessel
, built by Goa Shipyard Limited.
Booms,
skimmer
s and dispersants are used in oil-spill response; skimmers mechanically collect oil from the water surface.
GloLitter addresses marine plastic litter arising from shipping and fisheries, is funded by Norway and has India as a partner country.
Ghost nets are abandoned, lost or discarded fishing gear that continues to trap marine life.
The Gulf of Mexico is an example of a marine area affected by a hypoxic dead zone caused by nutrient runoff and eutrophication.
SACEP was established in 1982, GloLitter Partnerships began in 2019, the Ballast Water Management Convention came into force in 2017, and the Mayapuri incident occurred in 2010.

secs.t: Soil pollution - control, heavy metals → sources, DDT, fly ash

x: Floods, acid rain and mineral deposition are natural causes, while industrial waste, farm runoff, urban waste, mining, e-waste and coal ash are human causes of soil pollution.

Mercury is associated with chlor-alkali effluent and fungicides; cadmium with mining effluent, phosphate fertilisers and batteries; copper, zinc and lead with smelting and industrial waste; and chromates with tanneries and industrial waste.
Cadmium
contamination, arising among other sources from mining effluent, phosphate fertilisers and batteries, is associated with itai-itai disease.
MoEFCC requires fly ash to be used in bricks, cement and roads within
300 km
of thermal plants, thereby discouraging its dumping on soil.

secs.t: Bioremediation and green technologies

x: Biostimulation means adding nutrients to stimulate the activity of native pollutant-degrading microbes.
Bioremediation is eco-friendly and cheaper, but it can be slower than chemical treatment and its results vary with environmental conditions.
Oil Zapper is a consortium of bacteria from TERI that consumes oily sludge and crude oil from oil spills.

secs.t: Light pollution - dark sky reserves

x: Hanle in Ladakh became India's first Dark Sky Reserve in 2022 within Changthang Wildlife Sanctuary, while Pench Tiger Reserve became India's first Dark Sky Park in 2024.
Dark sky reserves require very little artificial light, clear and dry skies, a protected core with a buffer and community light-management rules.
Hanle's clear skies, least humidity, low pollution and high altitude make Ladakh suitable for astro-tourism.

secs.t: Thermal pollution - sources, effect on DO

x: Both statements are true, and the reduced oxygen-holding capacity of warmer water directly explains why dissolved oxygen falls with increasing temperature.
Sudden temperature changes can
stress or kill aquatic life
, while warmer water also holds less dissolved oxygen.
Cooling towers, cooling ponds, recirculating cooling water and regulated discharge temperatures help control thermal pollution.

secs.t: Noise control measures

x: Green mufflers are rows of trees and shrubs along roads that help absorb noise.
Traffic management, vehicle maintenance, loudspeaker limits and zoning around hospitals and schools are all stated noise-control measures.

secs.t: Tummalapalle uranium mining (AP)

x: The Tummalapalle uranium mine and mill of UCIL are located in
YSR Kadapa district
of Andhra Pradesh.
Villagers have alleged groundwater contamination and skin or health problems associated with the tailings pond at Tummalapalle.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The
Patna High Court
issued statewide directives on DJ trolleys and loudspeakers on 14 August 2026 after the Bihar State Pollution Control Board failed to enforce the prescribed limits.
The Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board operates 25 Real Time Noise Monitoring Stations, runs 9 Common Effluent Treatment Plants and promotes Zero Liquid Discharge.
